title: BaseLpVault.withdraw rounds share burn down, allowing over-withdrawal that dilutes other LPs
root_cause: `withdraw()` computes shares to burn via `convertToShares(assets)`, and `convertToShares` uses `Math.mulDiv(... )` with floor rounding. For exact-asset withdrawals, rounding down under-burns shares whenever `assets * totalSupply / totalAssets` is non-integer; ERC4626-style safety requires rounding up for withdraw paths.
trigger_scenario: Vault has non-integer price-per-share, e.g. `totalAssets=150` and `totalSupply=100` after hedging profit donation.
Attacker owns 50 shares (half of supply).
Attacker repeatedly calls `withdraw(2, attacker, attacker)`.
Each call burns `floor(2*100/150)=1` share but transfers 2 assets out.
After 50 calls, attacker burns 50 shares and withdraws 100 assets, even though fair value for 50 shares was 75 assets.
The extra 25 assets are transferred from remaining LPs (value extraction via rounding drift).
preconditions: `totalSupply() > 0` and `totalAssets()`/`totalSupply()` yields non-integer conversion for chosen withdrawal amounts.
Attacker can perform multiple withdrawals (or choose a single amount with favorable floor rounding).
Vault has enough `idleAssets()` to satisfy requested withdrawals.

title: ProtocolPool.withdraw: Owner can drain LP principal by withdrawing below totalShares -> LP fund_loss
root_cause: The owner's `withdraw()` function (line 187) only checks `balance - amount >= reservedTotal` but does NOT check that the remaining balance covers `totalShares` (LP principal). This means the owner can withdraw any idle funds including those backing LP shares, making the pool underwater and reducing LP redemption value below principal.
trigger_scenario: LP deposits 100 tokens via deposit(), getting 100 shares. Pool balance = 100, totalShares = 100, reservedTotal = 0.
Owner calls withdraw(payable(owner), 80). Check passes: balance(100) - amount(80) = 20 >= reservedTotal(0).
Pool now has 20 tokens, 100 totalShares. LP share value = 20/100 = 0.2 per share.
LP can only redeem 100 shares for 20 tokens instead of 100 tokens principal.
preconditions: Owner is trusted but potentially compromised or malicious
LP deposits exist (totalShares > 0)
reservedTotal is low relative to pool balance

title: ProtocolPool: Owner can withdraw surplus while pool is healthy, but LP deposits create false surplus -> fund_loss
root_cause: The `protocolSurplus()` function returns `balance - totalShares` when `balance > totalShares`. The owner `withdraw()` only checks `balance - amount >= reservedTotal`. Consider: if no reservations exist, the owner can withdraw up to `balance` tokens. There is no check that `balance - amount >= totalShares`. The `protocolSurplus` view is just informational and NOT enforced by `withdraw`. So the owner can drain LP principal even when the pool is healthy, not just surplus. The test `testAdminWithdrawReducesLpValue` confirms this: owner withdraws 30 from a pool with 100 LP deposits and no surplus, reducing LP value to 0.7.
trigger_scenario: LP deposits 100. balance = 100, totalShares = 100, reservedTotal = 0.
protocolSurplus() = 0 (no surplus).
Owner calls withdraw(owner, 100). Check: balance(100) - amount(100) = 0 >= reservedTotal(0). Passes.
Pool: balance = 0, totalShares = 100. LPs lost everything.
The test testAdminWithdrawReducesLpValue at line 465-474 explicitly documents this behavior.
preconditions: Owner is malicious or compromised
LP deposits exist
reservedTotal is 0 or low

title: RevealMarket.refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash: Function is a no-op that never updates the key hash -> loss_of_function
root_cause: refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash (RevealMarket line 678-684) checks that verifier.verifyingKeyHash() == lockedVerifierKeyHash (line 682), then only emits an event without updating lockedVerifierKeyHash. If the verifier's key has been legitimately rotated (e.g., via Verifier.setVerifyingKey), the new key hash will NOT match lockedVerifierKeyHash, causing the function to revert with VerifierKeyMismatch. If the keys DO match, the function is a no-op since it never writes a new value. This means there is no way to update lockedVerifierKeyHash after lockBatches is called, even if the verifier key is legitimately rotated. The only recovery path is enableRefunds (cancel the market).
trigger_scenario: Market is locked via lockBatches, setting lockedVerifierKeyHash to the current verifier key hash
Owner legitimately rotates the verifier key via Verifier.setVerifyingKey (bug fix, security upgrade)
Owner calls refreshMarketLockedVerifierKey to update the locked market's key hash
_validateVerifier passes (new key hash is in approvedVerifierKeyHash after re-approval)
rm.refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash() reverts because verifier.verifyingKeyHash() != lockedVerifierKeyHash
Settlement is permanently blocked for this market unless enableRefunds is called
preconditions: Market is in Phase.Locked
Verifier key has been rotated after lock
Owner needs to update the locked key hash to continue settlement

title: ProtocolPool._deposits: Unbounded deposit record growth causes gas DoS on lpWithdraw -> dos
root_cause: Each call to `deposit()` (line 235) pushes a new DepositRecord to `_deposits[msg.sender]`. Both `_unlockedSharesOf` (line 336-344) and `_burnUnlockedShares` (line 347-362) iterate ALL records for an LP with no compaction. Records with `shares == 0` are never removed. An LP (or attacker on behalf of an LP via a contract) who makes many small deposits can grow the array until gas costs for iteration exceed the block gas limit, permanently locking their shares.
trigger_scenario: Attacker creates a contract that calls deposit() in a loop with minimum amounts (e.g., 1 wei each).
After thousands of deposits, _deposits[attacker].length is very large.
When the attacker (or anyone checking maxRedeemable) calls lpWithdraw or unlockedShares, the loop iterates all records.
Gas cost exceeds block gas limit. lpWithdraw reverts. Funds are permanently locked.
preconditions: No minimum deposit amount enforced (amount == 0 is checked but 1 wei is valid)
Attacker has enough tokens for many tiny deposits
Block gas limit is finite (standard EVM constraint)

title: RevealMarket.setOracle: Oracle rotation allowed during Cancelled phase is meaningless but not harmful -> griefing
root_cause: setOracle (line 642-647) reverts only if phase == Locked || phase == Settled, allowing rotation during Commit and Cancelled phases. During Cancelled phase, the oracle has no functional role — enableRefunds has already been called, and no oracle actions (lockBatches, postResult, verifyAndSettle) are valid in Cancelled phase. The oracle address is stored but never used again. This is wasteful gas but not a security issue. It could be mildly confusing for off-chain monitors that track oracle changes.
trigger_scenario: Market is cancelled via enableRefunds
Factory owner calls updateOracle(market, newOracle) — succeeds
newOracle address is stored but has no functional impact
No security vulnerability, just unnecessary state change
preconditions: Market is in Cancelled phase

title: RevealMarket.claimWithOracleAuthorization: Oracle-signed payout is not bound to the committed leaf -> compromised oracle can drain all settled liquidity through one owned ticket
root_cause: claimWithOracleAuthorization() verifies only (ticketId, owner, payout, expiry) against an oracle signature and never recomputes the Poseidon commitment leaf or checks Merkle inclusion for the ticket. The only quantitative guard is claimedLiability <= totalLiability, so any oracle-signed payout amount is accepted even if it does not match the ticket's committed (outcome, amount, payout, salt) preimage.
trigger_scenario: Attacker commits at least one ticket in the market (winning or losing).
After settlement, the oracle key is compromised (or malicious oracle operator acts).
Attacker signs/obtains an oracle authorization for their own ticketId with payout equal to the entire remaining totalLiability and a valid expiry.
Attacker calls claimWithOracleAuthorization(ticketId, hugePayout, expiry, sig).
The contract marks the ticket claimed, updates claimedLiability, and transfers hugePayout to that ticket owner because no leaf/proof validation runs on this path.
Subsequent legitimate tickets fail to claim due to OverClaimed or depleted market balance.
preconditions: Oracle signing key is compromised or oracle is malicious.
Attacker controls at least one committed ticket owner address.

title: MarketFactory.setVerifierApproval: Revoking approval does not clear pinned codehash/keyHash -> loss_of_function
root_cause: setVerifierApproval(verifier, false) (line 200-203) sets approvedVerifier[verifier] = false but does NOT clear pinnedVerifierCodehash[verifier] or pinnedVerifierKeyHash[verifier]. If the verifier is later upgraded (key rotation via setVerifyingKey) and re-approved, the pinned values from the first approval will cause VerifierDrift revert (line 188) since the new verifyingKeyHash won't match the pinned value. This means once a verifier is approved and then revoked, it can NEVER be re-approved with a different key unless a new verifier contract is deployed. The approvedVerifierCodehash and approvedVerifierKeyHash are cleared on revocation (they're just set to 0 implicitly by the event emission, but actually they aren't cleared either — they retain their values). Actually re-reading: on revocation, only approvedVerifier is set to false. approvedVerifierCodehash and approvedVerifierKeyHash retain their values. On re-approval, the function reads pinnedVerifierCodehash which was set on first approval and never cleared.
trigger_scenario: Owner approves verifier V with keyHash K1 — pinnedVerifierCodehash[V] and pinnedVerifierKeyHash[V] are set
Owner revokes V: approvedVerifier[V] = false, but pinned values remain
Verifier owner rotates key: V now has keyHash K2 (via Verifier.setVerifyingKey)
Owner tries to re-approve V: setVerifierApproval(V, true)
pinnedVerifierCodehash check: codehash matches (same contract, not proxy) — passes
pinnedVerifierKeyHash[V] == K1 but verifier.verifyingKeyHash() == K2 — VerifierDrift revert
V cannot be re-approved without deploying a new verifier contract
preconditions: Verifier was previously approved with one key
Verifier key was rotated via setVerifyingKey
Owner attempts to re-approve the same verifier address

title: MarketFactory.setVerifierApproval: Pinned codehash persists permanently preventing same-address verifier upgrades -> loss_of_function
root_cause: When a verifier is first approved, pinnedVerifierCodehash[verifier] and pinnedVerifierKeyHash[verifier] are set permanently (line 186-187). These pinned values are NEVER cleared — not on revocation (line 200-203 only clears approvedVerifier), and not on any other admin action. This creates a permanent binding between the verifier address and its initial code+key. If the verifier's code is legitimately upgraded (e.g., a non-proxy verifier is SELFDESTRUCT+CREATE2 redeployed, or a new key is set), the pinned values will cause VerifierDrift on re-approval. The only workaround is deploying a fresh verifier contract at a new address. This is likely intentional as a safety measure (preventing code mutation), but it means verifier key rotation requires new contract deployment.
trigger_scenario: Verifier V is deployed and approved: pinnedCodehash[V] = CH1, pinnedKeyHash[V] = KH1
V.setVerifyingKey is called (legitimate key rotation): V now has keyHash KH2 but same codehash CH1
Owner revokes V: approvedVerifier[V] = false; pinned values remain CH1/KH1
Owner re-approves V: codehash check passes (CH1 == CH1), but keyHash check fails (KH2 != KH1)
VerifierDrift is thrown — V cannot be re-approved at this address
Must deploy new Verifier contract with the new key
preconditions: Verifier key was rotated after initial approval
Owner wants to re-approve the same verifier address

title: MarketFactory.setVerifierApproval + RevealMarket.refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash pin verifier keys in a way that can deadlock locked markets after verifier key rotation
root_cause: Factory governance permanently pins `approvedVerifierKeyHash` per verifier address, while `Verifier` allows owner key rotation. Once a market is locked, `refreshMarketLockedVerifierKey` does not actually write a new key hash (it only re-checks equality) and `setVerifier` is unavailable outside Commit phase, so a post-lock verifier key rotation creates an unrecoverable policy mismatch.
trigger_scenario: A market enters `Phase.Locked` and stores `lockedVerifierKeyHash` during `lockBatches`.
The verifier owner rotates the proving key via `Verifier.setVerifyingKey`, changing `verifyingKeyHash` without changing verifier address.
`MarketFactory.isVerifierCurrentlyApproved` starts returning false because on-chain key hash no longer matches pinned `approvedVerifierKeyHash`.

`MarketFactory.refreshMarketLockedVerifierKey` cannot repair the lock because `_validateVerifier` now fails on drift and `RevealMarket.refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash` requires equality instead of updating state.
Settlement entrypoints (`verifyAndSettle` / `verifyAndSettleBatched`) fail verifier approval/key checks, leaving market stuck in Locked until timeout-driven refunds.
preconditions: A locked market still needs settlement proofs.
Verifier key material is changed after market lock (maliciously or operationally).
Market cannot be moved back to Commit phase to rotate verifier address.

evidence.snippet: Pins verifier key hash per address and re-approval reverts on drift.
Checks current key equals locked key but never writes a new locked key hash.

title: RevealMarket.extendCommitDeadline: Missing expiry guard allows reopening commits after deadline, enabling late-position insertion before lock
root_cause: extendCommitDeadline() only checks monotonic increase and one-shot/max-range constraints, but never requires block.timestamp <= commitDeadline. Because commitWithAuthorization() gates on the mutable commitDeadline value, a factory owner can extend after the original deadline has already passed and reopen the commit window.
trigger_scenario: Users submit commitments until the original commitDeadline and stop because commit window appears closed.
Original deadline passes, but oracle has not yet called lockBatches().
Factory owner calls extendMarketCommitDeadline(), which forwards to RevealMarket.extendCommitDeadline() and sets a new future deadline without checking that the previous deadline already expired.
Relayer resumes commitWithAuthorization() calls because block.timestamp is now below the new commitDeadline.
Oracle can no longer lock immediately since lockBatches() now requires waiting for the extended deadline.
Late commitments are inserted with more information than earlier participants had, breaking market fairness and deadline finality assumptions.
preconditions: Market is still in Phase.Commit (not yet locked).
Original commit deadline has elapsed, and factory owner is willing to extend once.
Relayer continues accepting commits after extension.

evidence.snippet: extendCommitDeadline checks only newDeadline>commitDeadline, phase==Commit, one-shot flag, and max extension; no check that block.timestamp is still before current commitDeadline.
commitWithAuthorization allows commits whenever block.timestamp < commitDeadline, so extending commitDeadline re-opens commit acceptance.
lockBatches requires block.timestamp >= commitDeadline, so extension also delays locking and finalization.
Factory owner can invoke extendMarketCommitDeadline at any time while market remains in commit phase.

title: RevealMarket.setClaimsPaused/_effectiveClaimDeadline: Ongoing pause time extends claim deadline in real-time -> claims and sweep can be frozen indefinitely
root_cause: When claims are paused in Settled phase, _effectiveClaimDeadline() adds (block.timestamp - claimPauseStartedAt) continuously. claim() is blocked by claimsPaused, and sweepUnclaimed() requires block.timestamp > _effectiveClaimDeadline(). While paused, effective deadline moves forward with current time, so sweep condition can never become true until an explicit unpause occurs. No max pause duration or emergency sweep bypass exists.
trigger_scenario: Market reaches Settled and claimDeadline is initialized.
Factory owner calls setClaimsPaused(true), setting claimPauseStartedAt = now.
Users cannot call claim because ClaimsPaused reverts.
As time passes, _effectiveClaimDeadline grows by the same amount (now - claimPauseStartedAt), so it stays ahead of block.timestamp.
Factory cannot call sweepUnclaimed because ClaimWindowOpen keeps reverting while paused.
If pause is never lifted (operator failure, key loss, or malicious governance), both user claims and terminal sweeping are permanently blocked.
preconditions: Market is in Settled phase.
Claims are paused and not later unpaused by factory governance.

title: ProtocolPool.deposit: New LP deposits after draw dilute loss exposure unfairly -> unfair_treatment
root_cause: Shares are minted 1:1 regardless of pool health (line 231). After a draw makes the pool underwater (e.g., 60 assets, 100 shares), a new depositor adds 100 tokens and gets 100 shares. Pool becomes 160 assets, 200 shares. Share value = min(160/200, 1) = 0.8. The existing LP's loss deepens from 40% to 20%, but the new LP also immediately takes a 20% loss. This is by design (documented), but the new LP bears loss from draws that happened BEFORE they deposited, which is economically unfair.
trigger_scenario: LP1 deposits 100 tokens. Pool: 100 assets, 100 shares.
Market draws 40. Pool: 60 assets, 100 shares. LP1 share value = 0.6.
LP2 deposits 100 tokens (1:1 shares). Pool: 160 assets, 200 shares.
LP2's 100 shares are now worth 100 * 160/200 = 80. LP2 lost 20 tokens immediately.
LP1's 100 shares are now worth 100 * 160/200 = 80. LP1 recovered from 60 to 80 at LP2's expense.
preconditions: Pool is underwater (totalAssets < totalShares) due to prior draws
New LP deposits without knowing the pool is underwater
No front-end or contract-level warning about underwater state

title: ProtocolPool.deposit: 1:1 share minting after underwater state dilutes existing LP loss recovery -> unfair_treatment
root_cause: This is a concrete economic analysis of hyp-pool-004. When pool is underwater at ratio R = totalAssets/totalShares < 1, a new deposit of X tokens mints X shares (1:1). New totalAssets = oldAssets + X, new totalShares = oldShares + X. New ratio = (oldAssets + X)/(oldShares + X). Since oldAssets < oldShares, the new ratio is between R and 1. The new depositor immediately loses value: their X shares are worth X * newRatio < X. Meanwhile existing LPs see their share value increase from R to newRatio. This is a wealth transfer from the new LP to existing LPs. The magnitude depends on how underwater the pool is and the deposit size.
trigger_scenario: Pool: 50 assets, 100 shares. R = 0.5. Each share worth 0.5.
New LP deposits 100 tokens, gets 100 shares. Pool: 150 assets, 200 shares. R = 0.75.
New LP's 100 shares now worth 75 tokens (lost 25 immediately).
Old LP's 100 shares now worth 75 tokens (gained 25 from 50).
25 tokens transferred from new LP to old LP via dilution.
This is a known design trade-off (simplicity of 1:1 minting) but economically disadvantageous for new depositors.
preconditions: Pool is underwater (totalAssets < totalShares)
New LP deposits without adjusting for underwater state

title: ProtocolPool.lpWithdraw: After large draw, LP burn loop iterates many zero records before finding unlocked shares -> dos
root_cause: This is a refinement of hyp-pool-002 and hyp-pool-008 focused on the specific interaction pattern. If an LP has made many deposits, and many are already fully burned (shares = 0), the FIFO burn loop still iterates through all of them to find remaining unlocked shares. The loop condition `i < len && remaining > 0` continues even when `records[i].shares == 0` (it just skips via `continue` on the shares == 0 check in the condition `records[i].unlockTime > block.timestamp || records[i].shares == 0`). The worst case is when all early records are zeroed and the unlocked shares are at the end of the array.
trigger_scenario: LP makes 1000 small deposits over time. All unlock after 60 days.
LP partially withdraws many times, zeroing out the first 999 records.
LP tries to withdraw from the 1000th record.
_burnUnlockedShares iterates records 0-998 (all have shares == 0, skipped), reaches 999.
1000 iterations consume significant gas but likely within block limit for reasonable counts.
For very large arrays (100k+), this could become a real DoS.
preconditions: LP has accumulated many deposit records
Most early records are already burned (shares = 0)

title: RevealMarket.setClaimsPaused: Repeated pause/unpause cycles extend effective claim deadline indefinitely, bypassing MAX_CLAIM_DEADLINE_EXTENSION
root_cause: Each pause/unpause cycle in setClaimsPaused accumulates duration to claimPauseTotalDuration (line 705: claimPauseTotalDuration += block.timestamp - claimPauseStartedAt). The _effectiveClaimDeadline function (line 907) adds claimPauseTotalDuration to the base claimDeadline. While extendClaimDeadline has a one-time limit (claimDeadlineExtended flag) and MAX_CLAIM_DEADLINE_EXTENSION cap, the pause duration accumulation has no cap whatsoever. The factory owner can call setClaimsPaused(true) then setClaimsPaused(false) repeatedly to extend the effective claim deadline by arbitrary amounts, far beyond MAX_CLAIM_DEADLINE_EXTENSION.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market settles normally, claimDeadline is set to block.timestamp + 180 days.
Step 2: Factory owner calls setMarketClaimsPaused(market, true), recording claimPauseStartedAt = T1.
Step 3: After 365 days, factory owner calls setMarketClaimsPaused(market, false). claimPauseTotalDuration += 365 days.
Step 4: Factory owner immediately calls setMarketClaimsPaused(market, true) again.
Step 5: Repeat steps 3-4 indefinitely. Each cycle adds more time to claimPauseTotalDuration.
Step 6: The effective claim deadline is now years in the future, far exceeding MAX_CLAIM_DEADLINE_EXTENSION of 365 days.
preconditions: Market is in Settled phase.
Factory owner is malicious or compromised.

title: MarketFactory.owner: Single compromised owner key grants full protocol control -> fund_loss
root_cause: MarketFactory uses Ownable2Step with a single owner address as the trust root for all administrative operations. A compromised owner key can rotate oracles to post fraudulent results, rotate verifiers to forge proofs, rotate relayers to redirect user deposits, sweep unclaimed funds, and pause/unpause operations at will. There is no timelock, multisig enforcement, or role separation at the contract level.
trigger_scenario: Attacker compromises the factory owner private key (phishing, leaked key, compromised HSM)
Attacker calls updateOracle(market, maliciousOracle) to set a colluding oracle
Attacker calls updateMarketVerifier(market, maliciousVerifier, fakeCircuitHash) with a pre-approved malicious verifier
Malicious oracle calls lockBatches with fabricated roots, then postResult, then verifyAndSettle with a proof the malicious verifier accepts
Settlement finalizes with inflated totalLiability, draining the protocol pool via draw()
Alternatively, attacker calls sweepUnclaimed after claim deadline to drain settled market funds
preconditions: Owner private key is compromised
Attacker has access to submit transactions as the owner
Markets exist with active user funds (committed or settled)

title: RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization global ticketId binding enables relayer-ordering censorship of pre-approved commits
root_cause: The authorization object is bound to an exact `ticketId`, while `ticketId` is a single global queue (`commitments.length`) that can change between approval and execution. Because only `RelayerEscrow.owner()` can execute `commitOnBehalf`, the relayer fully controls sequencing and can invalidate previously approved authorizations by inserting other commits first.
trigger_scenario: Two users obtain backend-signed commit authorizations that both target the current next ticket id.
Both users call `approveCommitAuthorization`, storing hashes that include that specific ticket id.
Relayer owner executes one commit first via `commitOnBehalf`, incrementing `commitments.length` in `RevealMarket`.
The second user's authorized payload now fails `auth.ticketId == commitments.length` in `commitWithAuthorization` with `TicketIndexMismatch`.
By repeatedly choosing ordering (or withholding execution) the relayer can force selected users to re-sign/re-approve until the commit window closes.
preconditions: Commit execution is centralized through `RelayerEscrow.commitOnBehalf` (`onlyOwner`).
Authorizations are pre-signed for a concrete `ticketId` before on-chain execution.
There is contention or intentional ordering manipulation before `commitDeadline`.

title: RevealMarket._safeTransferExact: Strict balance-delta accounting can permanently DoS settlement/claims/refunds when collateral token behavior drifts
root_cause: All payout paths hard-revert unless sender and recipient balance deltas are exactly compatible with a no-fee, non-rebasing token. _safeTransferExact() enforces senderDebited == amount and recipientReceived >= amount using pre/post balanceOf checks. If token mechanics change post-deployment (fee-on-transfer toggle, blacklist side effects, rebasing quirks), claims/refunds/sweeps and even surplus forwarding during finalization can revert indefinitely.
trigger_scenario: Users commit funds and market reaches Locked or Settled lifecycle stages.
Collateral token behavior changes after deployment (e.g., transfer fee activation, blacklist semantics, unusual balance accounting).
Market executes _safeTransferExact() in _finalizeSettlement(), claim(), refund*(), or sweep*().
Pre/post balance checks fail strict invariants (senderDebited != amount or recipientReceived < amount).
Transaction reverts with FeeOnTransferNotSupported.
Because all outbound value paths share this helper, users can be stuck unable to claim or refund, and factory sweep fallback can also fail.
preconditions: Collateral token does not maintain strict no-fee/no-rebase semantics for the full market lifetime.
Market reaches a state requiring token outflow (settle, claim, refund, or sweep).

evidence.snippet: _safeTransferExact requires senderDebited == amount and recipientReceived >= amount based on balanceOf deltas; otherwise it reverts FeeOnTransferNotSupported.
_finalizeSettlement forwards surplus via _safeTransferExact(protocolPool, surplus), so finalization can fail on token semantic drift.
Claims, refunds, and sweep paths all rely on _safeTransferExact, expanding any token-compatibility failure into a full lifecycle payout DoS.

title: MarketFactory.setRelayerCommitsPaused is fail-open: pause fanout errors are swallowed so active relayers can remain live during emergency stop
root_cause: Emergency pause propagation uses nested `try/catch` and never reverts on failure; it only emits `RelayerPausePropagationFailed`. The outer function still emits global pause success even if one or more active relayers reject or ignore the pause call.
trigger_scenario: At least one market points to an active relayer in `activeRelayers`.
That relayer reverts or behaves non-standardly when `setCommitsPaused(true)` is called.
Owner invokes `setRelayerCommitsPaused(true)` expecting a protocol-wide commit stop.
`_setRelayerCommitsPausedBatch` catches the failure and continues without reverting the transaction.
The transaction emits pause events, but the failing relayer stays unpaused and can continue forwarding commits for its markets.
preconditions: An active relayer contract can fail/ignore pause updates (misconfiguration, upgrade drift, or malicious relayer implementation).
Operators rely on factory-level pause fanout as an emergency circuit breaker.

evidence.snippet: Pause propagation failures emit events but do not revert.
Global pause event is emitted after best-effort fanout, regardless of per-relayer failures.

title: ProtocolPool.lpWithdraw: LP sandwich attack around market draw() reduces victim LP value -> theft_of_yield
root_cause: When a market calls `draw()`, pool balance decreases, making all LP shares worth less via `_lpShareValue`. An attacker who sees a pending draw transaction could front-run by withdrawing their shares at full value, then back-run by re-depositing at the now-lower rate. However, the LOCK_DURATION of 60 days prevents immediate withdrawal of newly deposited shares. The question is whether an attacker with pre-existing unlocked shares can exploit this.
trigger_scenario: Attacker deposits 100 tokens. Waits 60 days until shares unlock.
Pool has 200 tokens total (100 from attacker, 100 from victim), totalShares = 200.
Attacker sees a pending draw(market, 100) transaction in the mempool.
Attacker front-runs by calling lpWithdraw(100) - gets 100 tokens at 1:1 (pool is healthy before draw).
draw(market, 100) executes. Pool now has 0 tokens, 100 shares. Victim LP shares are worthless.
Attacker avoids 50% of the loss that should have been shared equally.
preconditions: Attacker has unlocked shares (waited > 60 days since deposit)
A large draw transaction is pending in the mempool
Attacker can front-run (MEV, sequencer ordering)
Pool has sufficient idle liquidity for the withdrawal

title: RevealMarket.enableRefunds: Timeout cancel path can discard posted results and accepted batch proofs, allowing privileged settlement rollback
root_cause: enableRefunds() allows transition from Locked -> Cancelled solely on timeout, without checking resultPosted status or settledBatchCount progress. This lets a privileged factory caller void a market after outcome publication and partial proof acceptance, effectively overriding in-flight settlement state.
trigger_scenario: Market is locked and oracle posts the winning outcome via postResult().
Oracle submits one or more valid batch proofs through verifyAndSettleBatched(), so settledBatchCount and settled sums become non-zero, but not all batches are completed yet.
No final _finalizeSettlement() occurs before lockedAt + SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS.
Factory owner calls enableMarketRefunds(), which forwards to enableRefunds() and flips phase to Cancelled without inspecting resultPosted or partial settlement progress.
All claim paths are disabled by phase check (requires Settled), and only refund paths remain.
Users who should have asymmetric winner payouts are instead forced into symmetric ticket refunds, rolling back economic finality after result revelation.
preconditions: Phase is Locked and settlement timeout has elapsed.
Factory owner can call enableMarketRefunds().
Settlement is partially complete (or at least result is posted) but not finalized.

evidence.snippet: enableRefunds in Locked phase checks only timeout and then sets phase=Cancelled; it does not inspect resultPosted, settledBatchCount, or any settlement-progress fields.
postResult persists outcome (resultPosted=true), but cancellation path does not require this to be false.
_verifyBatchProof records partial progress (settledBatchCount and sums), which can still be abandoned by later enableRefunds timeout cancellation.

title: MarketFactory.migrateMarketRelayerBalances migrates global user escrow balances (not market-scoped), enabling cross-market collateral misrouting
root_cause: Relayer balances are stored per-user globally in `RelayerEscrow` (no market dimension), but `migrateMarketRelayerBalances` is invoked per market and moves `oldRelayer.balances(user)` in full. This couples one market's relayer migration to all of a user's collateral parked on the old relayer.
trigger_scenario: A user keeps collateral on an old relayer for multiple markets.
Factory owner rotates a single market to a new relayer and calls `migrateMarketRelayerBalances` for that market.
The function reads `oldRelayer.balances(user)` and withdraws the full amount, then credits it on the target relayer.
Other markets still tied to the old relayer lose access to that user's previously available escrow balance.
Commits for those markets fail until users manually rebalance collateral across relayers.
preconditions: A user balance on old relayer is intended to serve more than one market.
Factory performs per-market relayer migration using the provided helper.

evidence.snippet: Migrates `oldRelayer.balances(user)` (entire user balance) per user during a single-market migration.
Escrow accounting is `mapping(address => uint256)` without market-level partitioning.

title: Verifier.setVerifyingKey: G2 coordinate order is not canonicalized on-chain so a structurally valid but semantically wrong VK can be installed and brick verification
root_cause: _buildG2 stores beta/gamma/delta FQ2 limbs exactly as provided and _setVerifyingKey only checks non-infinity plus precompile acceptance. There is no canonicalization or on-chain recomputation against a pinned expected key hash at rotation time, so alternate serialization conventions (e.g., unswapped c0/c1 limbs) can pass curve-validity checks while representing a different verifying key.
trigger_scenario: Owner rotates the verifier key using raw vk JSON coordinates from a tool that uses a different FQ2 limb order than the contract expects.
setVerifyingKey calls _buildG2 and accepts the coordinates as-is.
Pairing.isValidG2Point returns success because the swapped point is still a valid curve point.
The contract updates _vk and emits VerifyingKeyUpdated, so governance believes rotation succeeded.
Subsequent valid Groth16 proofs generated for the intended circuit fail in verifyProof because on-chain vk no longer matches the circuit semantics.
Settlement paths that depend on this verifier revert/fail, effectively freezing proof-based finalization until another key rotation occurs.
preconditions: Key rotation is executed through tooling or manual input that does not enforce the verifier's exact FQ2 encoding convention.
The supplied coordinates remain curve-valid, so structural checks do not fail fast.

title: RelayerEscrow.approveCommitAuthorization creates non-revocable approvals that relayer owner can execute at arbitrary later times
root_cause: Approved commit authorizations are stored as a persistent boolean and there is no user-side revoke/cancel path. Execution timing is entirely delegated to `onlyOwner` `commitOnBehalf`, so approvals stay live until consumed (or naturally expired in market checks), even if user intent changes.
trigger_scenario: User approves a commit authorization with a long `expiry` via `approveCommitAuthorization`.
Relayer does not execute immediately and the approval remains `true` in `approvedCommitAuthorizations`.
User later changes intent but cannot revoke that authorization on-chain.
At any later point before expiry, relayer owner executes `commitOnBehalf` once user balance is sufficient.
User is forced into a commitment at relayer-chosen timing without a fresh consent transaction.
preconditions: A valid approval exists for `(user, authHash)` and has not been consumed.
`auth.expiry` has not elapsed when execution is attempted.
Relayer owner behaves adversarially or is compromised.

title: ProtocolPool.lpWithdraw: No slippage protection on withdrawal share value -> fund_loss
root_cause: The `lpWithdraw` function (line 244) computes `assets = convertToAssets(sharesToRedeem)` at execution time with no user-supplied minimum. Between the time an LP submits the withdrawal transaction and when it executes, a market `draw()` could reduce the pool balance, changing the share value. The LP receives fewer assets than expected with no ability to set a minimum acceptable amount.
trigger_scenario: LP has 100 unlocked shares. Pool: 200 assets, 200 shares. Expected redemption = 100 tokens.
LP submits lpWithdraw(100) transaction.
Before LP tx executes, market draw(100) executes. Pool: 100 assets, 200 shares.
LP tx executes: convertToAssets(100) = 100 * 100/200 = 50 tokens.
LP receives 50 tokens instead of expected 100, with no revert protection.
preconditions: LP has unlocked shares and submits a withdrawal
A draw transaction lands before the LP's withdrawal in the same or subsequent block
No off-chain slippage check or minAssets parameter available

title: RevealMarket.refundTicket: Permissionless refund path allows griefing by force-refunding tickets before the user wants
root_cause: refundTicket (line 545-557) is fully permissionless — anyone can call it with any valid ticketId when the market is Cancelled. The refund goes to commitmentUsers[ticketId], so the funds arrive at the correct destination. However, there could be scenarios where a user does not want the refund at that time (e.g., if they are using the commitment as collateral for something else off-chain, or if they prefer to leave funds in the contract temporarily). Since the refund marks claimedTickets[ticketId] = true, this is a one-shot operation. In practice, the only real griefing vector is gas cost to the caller, and the user receives their funds, so this is a low-severity issue.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market is cancelled and enters refund phase.
Step 2: Griefer calls refundTicket(ticketId) for every ticket in the market.
Step 3: All ticket owners receive their refunds immediately, whether they wanted them or not.
Step 4: The griefer spends gas but each refund goes to the correct commitmentUsers[ticketId].
preconditions: Market is in Cancelled phase.
Griefer has ETH for gas costs.

title: ProtocolPool.setMarketFactory: No factory-lock allows repeated override of marketFactory -> fund_loss
root_cause: ProtocolPool.setMarketFactory (line 88-92) is onlyOwner and has NO lock preventing the factory from being changed after initial set (unlike RelayerEscrow which has a FactoryLocked check at line 67). The ProtocolPool owner can change marketFactory at any time to point to a malicious factory contract. The malicious factory could then call registerMarket to whitelist arbitrary addresses, and those addresses could call draw() to drain the pool. However, draw() checks msg.sender == market (line 152), so the malicious 'market' address would need to be the caller itself, which it controls.
trigger_scenario: ProtocolPool owner (same as factory owner in normal setup) is compromised
Attacker calls protocolPool.setMarketFactory(maliciousFactory)
maliciousFactory calls protocolPool.registerMarket(attackerContract, largeCap)
attackerContract calls protocolPool.reserveLiability(attackerContract, amount) — passes because allowedMarket[attackerContract] is true and msg.sender == attackerContract
attackerContract calls protocolPool.draw(attackerContract, amount) — drains pool funds to attackerContract
Pool is drained of all unreserved funds
preconditions: ProtocolPool owner key is compromised
ProtocolPool has funds deposited

title: RelayerEscrow/ProtocolPool assume non-rebasing collateral; supply rebases can violate backing and reservation invariants across contracts
root_cause: Cross-contract accounting is done in raw token amounts (`balances`, `accountedCollateral`, `reservedTotal`, `reservedLiability`) with no share-based normalization and no token capability gate beyond fee-on-transfer checks. If collateral token balances change asynchronously (negative/positive rebasing), internal accounting can diverge from actual transferable balance.
trigger_scenario: Protocol deploys with an ERC20 that can rebase balances without transfers.
Users deposit into relayer escrow and markets reserve pool liability under pre-rebase balances.
A negative rebase reduces actual token balances in escrow/pool while `balances`, `accountedCollateral`, and reservation state remain unchanged.
Escrow withdraw/commit transfers and pool draw/withdraw checks begin reverting due insufficient real balance relative to accounting expectations.
Users/markets face withdrawal and settlement DoS until external recapitalization occurs.
preconditions: Collateral token supports asynchronous supply/balance rebasing or similar non-standard balance mutation.
Protocol does not hard-restrict collateral to strictly non-rebasing ERC20 implementations.

evidence.snippet: Excess is computed from `balanceOf - accountedCollateral` with no share/rebase adaptation.
Reservations rely on instantaneous `balanceOf` and `reservedTotal` invariants in raw token units.

title: RevealMarket.refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash: Locked verifier anchor is non-recoverable, so key drift hard-locks settlement until cancellation
root_cause: lockBatches snapshots lockedVerifierKeyHash once, and both verify paths require exact equality forever. The so-called refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash() path only re-checks equality and emits an event; it never updates the stored anchor. If verifier key hash drifts for operational reasons, market settlement becomes unrecoverable in Locked phase and can only exit via timeout cancellation.
trigger_scenario: Market is locked and stores lockedVerifierKeyHash from current verifier.
Verifier key hash changes later (e.g., emergency rotation, verifier redeploy policy mismatch, or ownership/governance maintenance event).
verifyAndSettle()/verifyAndSettleBatched() revert due VerifierNotApproved or VerifierKeyMismatch checks.
Factory attempts refreshMarketLockedVerifierKey(), but market.refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash() enforces current key == lockedVerifierKeyHash and does not write new state.
Settlement cannot progress even before any batch proof is accepted.
After timeout, only cancellation/refund path remains, sacrificing intended settlement finality.
preconditions: Phase is Locked with unsettled batches.
Verifier key hash no longer matches lockedVerifierKeyHash.
Factory cannot or does not finalize before timeout.

evidence.snippet: Locked key hash is captured once at lock and enforced by both settlement entry points.
refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash checks equality and emits an event, but never updates lockedVerifierKeyHash.
Factory refresh helper delegates to the no-op refresh path; there is no alternate state transition to rotate locked key anchor.

title: BaseLpVault outbound transfers are assumed exact, so non-standard assets can desynchronize accounting and real balances
root_cause: The vault validates exact amounts only on inbound `safeTransferFrom` paths (`deposit`, `repayFromHedge`) but does not enforce exact sender/receiver deltas for outbound `safeTransfer` paths (`withdraw`, `redeem`, `borrowForHedge`). If the configured 6-decimal asset has directional fees/surcharges/burn semantics on outbound transfers, internal accounting (`utilizedAssets`, burned shares) assumes exact movement while token balances realize different movement.
trigger_scenario: Vault is deployed with a 6-decimal token that behaves non-standard on outbound transfers (e.g., sender surcharge or recipient haircut).
LP calls `withdraw`/`redeem` or hedger calls `borrowForHedge`.
Vault updates state as if `amount` moved exactly (burns shares or increments `utilizedAssets`).
Token transfer applies non-standard fee behavior so actual debited/received value differs from `amount`.
Vault accounting diverges from real balances, causing LP underpayment, utilization mismeasurement, or insolvency drift.
preconditions: Configured `ASSET` is not strict vanilla USDC behavior on outbound transfers.
Outbound transfer paths (`withdraw`, `redeem`, or `borrowForHedge`) are exercised.

title: RevealMarket.claimWithOracleAuthorization: Missing per-ticket nonce/version lets stale low-value signatures be frontrun -> ticket can be permanently underpaid
root_cause: Oracle claim authorizations include payout and expiry but no monotonic nonce/version tracked per ticket. The contract accepts the first valid signature submitted and sets claimedTickets[ticketId] = true, so older signatures remain valid until expiry and cannot be revoked on-chain.
trigger_scenario: Oracle issues a first authorization for ticketId with payout P1 (for example during an initial off-chain calculation).
Oracle later issues a corrected authorization for the same ticket with payout P2 > P1.
Both signatures are observable by third parties (API leak, relayer logs, or mempool exposure).
An attacker submits the stale P1 signature first via claimWithOracleAuthorization.
The contract marks the ticket as claimed and transfers only P1.
The corrected P2 authorization becomes unusable because TicketAlreadyClaimed now blocks all further claims for that ticket.
preconditions: More than one valid oracle authorization exists for the same ticketId.
At least one stale/lower authorization is still unexpired when submitted.

title: ProtocolPool._burnUnlockedShares: Zeroed-out deposit records are never cleaned up -> dos
root_cause: When `_burnUnlockedShares` consumes a deposit record fully, it sets `records[i].shares = 0` (line 355) but never removes the record from the array. Over time, with repeated deposits and withdrawals, the array accumulates many zero-share records. Both `_unlockedSharesOf` and `_burnUnlockedShares` iterate ALL records including zeroed ones. This is a milder version of hyp-pool-002 but occurs organically through normal usage: each deposit-withdraw cycle leaves a dead record, gradually increasing gas cost for the LP.
trigger_scenario: LP makes deposit #1, waits, withdraws. Record[0].shares = 0.
LP makes deposit #2, waits, withdraws. Record[1].shares = 0.
After N cycles, _deposits[lp].length = N, all with shares = 0 except possibly the latest.
Each new lpWithdraw or unlockedShares call must iterate N records.
Eventually gas becomes prohibitive for routine operations.
preconditions: LP repeatedly deposits and fully withdraws over time
No mechanism exists to compact or clean dead records

title: RevealMarket.claimWithOracleAuthorization: Oracle can authorize arbitrary payout amounts up to totalLiability, bypassing ZK proof verification
root_cause: claimWithOracleAuthorization (line 561-599) does not verify the payout against the Merkle tree or ZK proof. The oracle signs a payout amount, and the only constraint is claimedLiability + payout <= totalLiability. A compromised oracle can sign payouts for the full totalLiability for a single ticket, draining all funds meant for other winners. The oracle is a trusted party, but this represents a single point of failure that could drain the entire market payout pool.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market settles with totalLiability = 100 ETH spread across many winning tickets.
Step 2: Compromised oracle signs a claimWithOracleAuthorization for ticketId=0 with payout = 100 ETH.
Step 3: Attacker calls claimWithOracleAuthorization(0, 100 ETH, expiry, oracleSig).
Step 4: claimedLiability += 100 ETH, which equals totalLiability, so the check passes.
Step 5: All 100 ETH is transferred to the owner of ticket 0. Other winning ticket holders cannot claim (OverClaimed).
preconditions: Oracle private key is compromised.
Market is in Settled phase with unclaimed liability.

title: MarketFactory: No timelock on admin operations allows instant malicious changes without community notice -> fund_loss
root_cause: All MarketFactory admin functions execute immediately with no timelock or delay mechanism. Critical operations like oracle rotation, verifier rotation, relayer rotation, sweep operations, and enabling refunds take effect in the same block they are called. In a scenario where the owner key is compromised, the attacker has zero-delay access to all admin functions. Industry best practice for high-value DeFi protocols is to use a timelock (e.g., 24-48 hour delay) on sensitive admin operations, giving the community time to detect and respond to unauthorized changes. Ownable2Step provides protection against accidental ownership transfer but not against a fully compromised key.
trigger_scenario: Owner key is compromised via phishing or key extraction
Attacker immediately calls updateOracle to set malicious oracle
Attacker calls updateMarketVerifier to set colluding verifier
No timelock delay means the community has zero blocks to detect and respond
Attacker settles markets with fraudulent proofs before anyone notices
Comparison: a 24h timelock would give monitoring systems time to alert and the backup key to intervene
preconditions: Owner key is compromised
No external timelock wrapper is deployed around the factory

title: Verifier.setVerifyingKey: single-step privileged key rotation has no staged activation, enabling immediate protocol-wide settlement freeze on shared verifier instances
root_cause: setVerifyingKey performs an immediate in-place replacement of _vk, _ic, circuitHash, and verifyingKeyHash in one owner transaction with no timelock, grace period, dual-approval, or staged next-key activation. Any mistake or compromised owner action instantly mutates the verifier anchor for every consumer using the same verifier address.
trigger_scenario: Multiple active markets rely on one Verifier address and have operational assumptions tied to the current verifyingKeyHash.
Owner key is compromised, or owner executes an incorrect/untimely rotation.
Attacker/operator calls setVerifyingKey with new key material.
verifyingKeyHash and circuitHash change atomically in the same transaction.
Downstream settlement calls that require the previous key anchor fail immediately after rotation.
Markets cannot finalize until governance performs additional recovery actions, creating a liveness outage window.
preconditions: Verifier ownership is a single high-privilege trust boundary without enforced timelock/multisig in this contract.
The verifier contract is shared by active markets that depend on stable key identity.

title: ProtocolPool LP unlock accounting is unbounded per-user, enabling withdrawal liveness failure via deposit-fragmentation
root_cause: Each `deposit()` appends a new `DepositRecord` and records are never compacted/removed. `lpWithdraw`, `unlockedShares`, and `maxRedeemable` iterate the full per-user `_deposits` array. This creates O(n) gas with unbounded n, so sufficiently fragmented deposit history can make redemption paths exceed block gas limits.
trigger_scenario: An LP (or automation acting for the LP) performs a very large number of small deposits over time.
After lock expiry, LP calls `lpWithdraw` to redeem unlocked shares.
`_burnUnlockedShares` scans the entire `_deposits[lp]` array and may run out of gas before completion.
The same O(n) scan affects `maxRedeemable` and `unlockedShares` queries, degrading front-end and keeper operations.
LP funds become practically stuck until transaction gas limits increase or custom off-chain splitting strategy is used.
preconditions: Per-user deposit record count grows large (many fragmented deposits).
User must rely on loop-based withdrawal path over full historical records.

title: Verifier.verifyProof: bool-return API is fail-hard for malformed proofs because decode and curve validation reverts are outside the catch boundary
root_cause: verifyProof only wraps this._pairingCheck(...) in try/catch. Earlier stages (_decodeProof, _buildG1/_buildG2, _validateG1Point, _validateG2Point) revert on malformed calldata or invalid points via InvalidProofEncoding/FieldOverflow/InvalidCurvePoint, so invalid proofs do not uniformly return false despite the interface's bool semantics.
trigger_scenario: A relayer or integrator accepts proof payloads from an untrusted source and calls verifyProof via a state-changing workflow.
Attacker submits proof bytes with malformed encoding length or off-curve coordinates.
verifyProof hits _decodeProof or _validateG*Point and reverts before entering the try/catch around _pairingCheck.
The parent transaction bubbles the revert instead of receiving a simple false result.
If the parent batches multiple proofs in one transaction, one malformed element aborts the entire batch execution.
An attacker can repeatedly inject malformed payloads to create operational griefing for automated submitters that expect soft-fail boolean behavior.
preconditions: Upstream workflow treats verifyProof as a non-reverting boolean filter and does not pre-simulate malformed payloads.
Proof submissions can be influenced by adversarial actors.

title: ProtocolPool.setCapacity: Capacity can only be set when reservedTotal == 0, risking permanent capacity lock -> loss_of_function
root_cause: The `setCapacity` function (line 197-203) reverts with `ActiveReservations()` if `reservedTotal != 0`. If there are always active market reservations (markets in Locked phase), the owner can never update capacity. In a busy protocol with many concurrent markets, `reservedTotal` may never reach zero, permanently preventing capacity management changes.
trigger_scenario: Owner sets capacity to 1000 via setCapacity(1000).
Market A reserves 500 (reservedTotal = 500).
Owner wants to increase capacity to 2000, calls setCapacity(2000).
Reverts with ActiveReservations() because reservedTotal = 500.
Market B reserves another 300 before Market A settles.
reservedTotal never reaches 0 due to overlapping market lifecycles.
Owner cannot update capacity settings.
preconditions: Multiple markets with overlapping lock/settlement windows
reservedTotal never reaches zero
Owner needs to adjust capacity settings

title: RevealMarket._verifyLeaf path depends on unverified lockBatches roots -> oracle+relayer can make trustless claims impossible and force trusted payout path
root_cause: claim() requires both commitments[ticketId] == leaf and a Merkle proof to batchRoots[batchIndex], but lockBatches() never recomputes/validates roots from on-chain commitments. It only checks counts and a relayer-owner signature over supplied roots. If supplied roots do not correspond to stored commitments, users cannot satisfy _verifyLeaf even with correct preimages.
trigger_scenario: Users commit valid ticket leaves, which are stored in commitments[].
At lock time, oracle submits batch roots that are inconsistent with commitments[] but still passes count checks.
Relayer owner signature is provided (collusion, compromise, or blind signing of incorrect roots).
Settlement completes against those roots.
Winning users call claim with correct (ticketId, outcome, amount, payout, salt) and fail InvalidMerkleProof because no proof can satisfy both commitment equality and mismatched batch root.
Only claimWithOracleAuthorization remains, shifting payout correctness from cryptographic leaf membership to trusted oracle signatures.
preconditions: Oracle submits incorrect batch roots during lock.
Relayer owner signs or is compromised for those roots.

title: Pairing precompile wrappers forward gas() with fail-revert semantics, enabling high-cost griefing when automated submitters relay attacker-controlled malformed proofs
root_cause: Pairing.add/scalarMul/pairing forward all remaining gas into precompile staticcalls and use require(success, ...). On failure paths, large gas chunks can be consumed before reverting, and Verifier only soft-catches the final _pairingCheck call. There is no on-chain gas cap or cheap pre-screening path for untrusted off-chain proof submissions.
trigger_scenario: An attacker feeds malformed proof payloads into a keeper/relayer pipeline that auto-submits settlement transactions.
The relayer submits transactions calling workflows that reach Verifier.verifyProof.
Precompile calls in Pairing consume substantial gas on failing validations/pairing operations.
The transaction reverts or returns false only after expensive cryptographic calls have run.
Attacker repeats submissions with varied malformed payloads.
Keeper operating budget is drained and settlement liveness degrades due repeated high-cost failures.
preconditions: An automated submitter relays proofs from untrusted sources without strict off-chain simulation/validation.
Adversary can continuously supply malformed proof attempts.

title: ProtocolPool.draw: Unreserved draw + capacity deduction without corresponding release creates capacity leak -> loss_of_function
root_cause: In the unreserved draw path (line 163-168), when `reserved == 0` and capacity is enabled, `capacity -= amount`. But `releaseLiabilityReservation` only adds back `reservedLiability[market]` to capacity. Since no reservation was made, the release function returns early (reserved == 0, line 136-137). The capacity deducted by the unreserved draw is NEVER restored. Over time, repeated unreserved draws permanently reduce capacity toward zero, even if the pool's actual balance recovers (e.g., via surplus returns).
trigger_scenario: Owner sets capacity = 1000.
Market A does NOT call reserveLiability. Calls draw(marketA, 200) directly.
Draw succeeds via unreserved path. capacity -= 200. capacity = 800.
Market A settles. Calls releaseLiabilityReservation(marketA). reservedLiability[marketA] == 0. Returns early.
capacity remains 800. The 200 is permanently lost from capacity.
Repeat: Market B draws 300 unreserved. capacity = 500. Never restored.
Eventually capacity = 0. No more draws possible even though pool has funds.
preconditions: Capacity is enabled (capacityEnabled = true)
Markets use the unreserved draw path (don't call reserveLiability first)
This appears to be by design for the RevealMarket flow (which always reserves via lockBatches), but could affect legacy or misconfigured markets

title: RevealMarket.claimWithOracleAuthorization: Oracle can sign different payout amounts for the same ticket, and the first executed determines the payout
root_cause: The oracle could sign two valid authorizations for the same ticketId with different payout values (e.g., payout=1 ETH and payout=2 ETH). Whichever is executed first determines the actual payout. Since there is no canonical expected payout enforced on-chain (unlike claim() which verifies via Merkle proof), the oracle has discretion over payout amounts. If the oracle signs a lower payout than the user deserves, the user receives less. If the oracle signs a higher payout, it may cause OverClaimed for later claimants. The only guard is claimedLiability <= totalLiability. This is a trust assumption on the oracle for the fallback path.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: User's winning ticket should pay 1 ETH based on the Merkle tree.
Step 2: Oracle signs two authorizations: one for 0.5 ETH and one for 1.5 ETH.
Step 3: If 0.5 ETH authorization is executed first, user loses 0.5 ETH they deserved.
Step 4: If 1.5 ETH authorization is executed first, 0.5 ETH extra is taken from the pool, potentially causing OverClaimed for another winner.
preconditions: Oracle acts maliciously or makes an error in payout computation.
User relies on claimWithOracleAuthorization instead of standard claim.

title: MarketFactory.updateMarketRelayer: Old relayer unregisterMarket failure is silently caught -> griefing
root_cause: updateMarketRelayer (line 275-278) calls oldRelayer.unregisterMarket(market) in a try/catch block. If unregisterMarket reverts (e.g., old relayer is self-destructed, or the old relayer's marketFactory was changed), the failure is silently caught and only RelayerUnregisterFailed is emitted. The market remains registered on the old relayer's allowedMarket mapping. This means the old relayer would still accept commits for this market via commitOnBehalf, even though the market's relayerEscrow now points to the new relayer. However, commitWithAuthorization on the market checks msg.sender == relayerEscrow (the new one), so commits from the old relayer would revert at the market level. The stale allowedMarket entry is a bookkeeping issue, not a fund risk.
trigger_scenario: Factory owner rotates market M1 from relayer R1 to R2
oldRelayer.unregisterMarket(M1) reverts because R1's marketFactory was changed to a different factory
RelayerUnregisterFailed event is emitted, execution continues
R1.allowedMarket[M1] remains true, but M1.relayerEscrow is now R2
If R1's owner tries commitOnBehalf for M1, the commit reaches M1 which checks msg.sender == R2, reverting
No fund loss, but stale state in R1
preconditions: Old relayer's unregisterMarket reverts for any reason
Market is being rotated to a new relayer

title: RelayerEscrow._safeTransferExact and RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization trust token-reported balances, enabling phantom collateral if token is adversarial
root_cause: Collateral movement and backing checks are validated only via `IERC20.balanceOf` deltas from the same external token contract being checked. If the token is upgradeable/non-standard and can lie about balances, `_safeTransferExact` and market backing predicates can be satisfied without an economically equivalent transfer.
trigger_scenario: Collateral token implementation is upgraded or deployed with adversarial `balanceOf` semantics.
`commitOnBehalf` calls `_safeTransferExact`, and token reports sender/recipient deltas consistent with an exact transfer even when real spendable balances did not move equivalently.
`commitWithAuthorization` passes `balanceOf(address(this)) >= totalEscrow + ticketSize` using the same manipulated view.
Escrow debits user accounting and market records commitment/rake based on assumed payment.
At settlement/claim time, liabilities are under-backed in real token terms, leading to insolvency or payout failure.
preconditions: Collateral token is non-standard, malicious, or mutable (e.g., upgradeable) and can return deceptive balances.
Protocol relies exclusively on token-reported balances for transfer correctness and payment backing.
Commits continue under this token behavior before detection.

title: Factory routing rotations are non-atomic across dependencies, leaving stale `allowedMarket` permissions and cross-contract authorization drift
root_cause: Dependency rotations only apply forward registration on the new endpoint, while old endpoint cleanup is missing (`updateMarketProtocolPool`) or best-effort only (`updateMarketRelayer` with swallowed unregister failures). This permits stale `allowedMarket` trust edges to outlive factory routing state.
trigger_scenario: A market is deployed and registered in initial relayer/pool allowlists.
Factory rotates the market to new dependencies.
Old relayer unregister can fail without reverting, and old protocol pool is never explicitly de-authorized.
Factory/market now reference new dependencies, but old dependencies still retain market-level authorization flags.
Subsequent operational rollbacks, misrouting, or unexpected call paths can exercise stale permissions that operators assume were revoked.
preconditions: At least one dependency rotation occurs for an existing market.
Operators assume de-registration is strict and atomic across all protocol-owned dependencies.

evidence.snippet: Old relayer unregister failures are caught and rotation continues.
New pool registration occurs with no corresponding old pool de-registration path.

title: RevealMarket claim/refund payout recipient is immutable ticket owner -> blacklist/frozen addresses become unclaimable and are swept to protocol pool
root_cause: All payout paths transfer only to the recorded ticket owner (or provided user constrained by _ticketOwner check) and provide no alternate recipient or rescue mechanism. If collateral token policy blocks transfers to that address (blacklist/freeze/compliance lock), claim/refund always reverts. After deadlines, sweeps move leftover market balance to protocolPool, effectively confiscating unclaimable user funds.
trigger_scenario: User commits a ticket and becomes the recorded owner in commitmentUsers[].
Before claiming/refunding, collateral token marks that address as blocked (or otherwise non-receivable).
User (or relayer) attempts claim/refund; _safeTransferExact reverts because token transfer to owner fails.
Ticket remains unclaimed as deadlines continue.
After claim/refund window closes, factory executes sweepUnclaimed or sweepCancelledRefunds.
Remaining balance, including the blocked user's entitlement, is transferred to protocolPool.
preconditions: Collateral token can block/freeze transfers for specific recipient addresses.
Affected ticket owner is blocked before successful claim/refund.

title: Pairing.isValidG2Point: verifier soundness is delegated entirely to precompile success semantics, so non-compliant BN254 implementations can silently weaken validation
root_cause: G2 validation and final proof checking rely on bn254 precompiles (0x08) as the sole correctness oracle. isValidG2Point accepts any input where staticcall succeeds and performs no independent subgroup/consistency checks in Solidity. If a chain/client implementation deviates from EIP-197 failure behavior, malformed twist points can be accepted.
trigger_scenario: Protocol deploys to an environment where bn254 precompile behavior is non-standard or buggy (e.g., missing strict subgroup checks).
Attacker provides malformed G2 data that should be rejected under canonical EIP-197 rules.
Pairing.isValidG2Point returns true because staticcall reports success on that environment.
Verifier accepts malformed key material during rotation or malformed proof points during verification.
pairing checks can then evaluate over invalid group elements, breaking Groth16 soundness assumptions.
Attacker may produce false-positive proof acceptance or induce systemic verification failure depending on the exact precompile deviation.
preconditions: Deployment target does not enforce canonical bn254 precompile validity checks.
Attacker can submit crafted proof/key material to the verifier workflow.

title: HedgeStrategyExecutor executes signed borrows without enforcing minOut/slippage against realized hedge outcome
root_cause: `Order.minOut` is never used for any on-chain condition and `Order.maxSlippageBps` is only compared to a global admin cap, not to any observed execution result. `executeBorrow` only moves funds from vault to receiver, so signed price-protection fields are not cryptographically bound to downstream execution quality.
trigger_scenario: Signer issues a valid order with conservative `minOut` / `maxSlippageBps` expecting slippage protection.
Any caller submits `executeBorrow` with that signature.
Executor validates signature, nonce, deadline, amount, and receiver allowlist, then borrows funds to receiver.
No on-chain check compares downstream hedge fill to `minOut` or realized slippage.
If receiver-side execution is compromised or adverse, vault funds are still borrowed with no protocol-level slippage enforcement.
preconditions: Receiver is allowed and order signature is valid.
Downstream hedge execution happens off-contract (or not at all), outside enforceable checks in `executeBorrow`.

title: RevealMarket.verifyAndSettleBatched: Partial batch settlement never completed -> Market stuck in Locked phase permanently
root_cause: In verifyAndSettleBatched (lines 418-442), _finalizeSettlement is only called when `settledBatchCount == batchCount` (line 438). If the oracle submits proofs for some batches but never submits the remaining ones, the market remains in Phase.Locked indefinitely. There is a mitigation via `enableRefunds()` (line 473) which allows the factory owner to cancel the market after `SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (14 days) from `lockedAt`, but this requires factory owner intervention and leaves users unable to claim winning payouts.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market is locked with multiple batches (e.g., 3 batches).
Step 2: Oracle posts the result and submits proofs for batch 0 and batch 1.
Step 3: Oracle goes offline or refuses to submit proof for batch 2.
Step 4: Market remains in Phase.Locked. Users cannot claim because phase != Settled.
Step 5: After 14 days, factory owner can call enableRefunds() to move to Cancelled phase, allowing refunds at ticketSize (full amount including rake).
preconditions: Oracle must go offline or be compromised after partial settlement
Multi-batch market (more than 1 batch)

title: ProtocolPool.reserveLiability: Direct token transfers inflate balance allowing over-reservation -> protocol_insolvency
root_cause: The `reserveLiability` function (line 121-122) checks `balance = COLLATERAL_TOKEN.balanceOf(address(this))` and verifies `amount <= balance - reservedTotal`. If someone sends tokens directly to the pool (not via deposit), the balance increases but no shares are minted and no accounting is updated. This inflated balance allows more liability to be reserved than the pool can actually cover from deposited capital. If all reserved liability is drawn, the pool could be drained below totalShares, harming LPs with unsocialized losses.
trigger_scenario: Pool has 100 tokens from LP deposits. totalShares = 100, reservedTotal = 0.
Someone sends 50 tokens directly to the pool contract (e.g., accidental transfer). Balance = 150.
Market reserves 150 via reserveLiability. reservedTotal = 150. Check passes: 150 <= 150 - 0.
Market draws 150. Pool balance drops to 0. LPs had 100 shares but pool has 0 tokens.
The 50 extra tokens were not LP deposits but are now lost to market draws.
preconditions: Tokens are sent directly to the pool outside the deposit() path
Multiple markets exist that can consume the inflated balance through reservations and draws

title: RevealMarket.sweepUnclaimed: Transfers entire token balance including unclaimed payouts, permanently locking user funds
root_cause: sweepUnclaimed (line 791-804) transfers the entire IERC20 balance to protocolPool after the effective claim deadline. If any winning ticket holders have not claimed by that time, their payouts are irrevocably lost. The function does not check (totalLiability - claimedLiability) or set aside unclaimed amounts. However, this is mitigated by the 180-day CLAIM_WINDOW_SECONDS plus pause extension, making it a known design choice. The concern is the interaction with pause duration: if setClaimsPaused is true when sweepUnclaimed is called, the effective deadline computation adds (block.timestamp - claimPauseStartedAt) which means sweepUnclaimed can still execute while claims are paused if enough wall time has passed since the pause started, as long as block.timestamp > _effectiveClaimDeadline().
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market settles with totalLiability = 10 ETH. Multiple users have winning tickets.
Step 2: Some users claim their payouts. claimedLiability = 5 ETH. 5 ETH remains in contract.
Step 3: Factory owner pauses claims via setClaimsPaused(true).
Step 4: Time passes beyond the effective claim deadline (claimDeadline + claimPauseTotalDuration + (block.timestamp - claimPauseStartedAt)).
Step 5: Factory owner calls sweepUnclaimed, which checks block.timestamp > _effectiveClaimDeadline() and proceeds.
Step 6: But claims are still paused! Users who haven't claimed cannot claim, and the sweep removes all remaining funds.
preconditions: Market is in Settled phase.
Some winning users have not yet claimed.
Factory owner pauses claims and waits long enough for the effective deadline to expire.

title: RevealMarket.claimWithOracleAuthorization: Oracle signature does not bind to the committed leaf, allowing the oracle to authorize payouts for tickets that don't match the Merkle tree
root_cause: claimWithOracleAuthorization (lines 576-591) constructs a signature digest that includes address(this), marketId, ticketId, user, winningOutcomeId, payout, expiry, chainid, and 'CLAIM_ORACLE_V1'. Notably, it does NOT include the commitment hash or verify it against the Merkle tree. This means the oracle can authorize a payout that differs from what the Merkle tree would specify. The oracle is fully trusted to determine the correct payout. This is by design as a fallback for when users cannot reconstruct their preimage, but it means the oracle has unilateral authority over payout amounts (bounded only by totalLiability). Combined with hyp-claim-014, this is a significant trust assumption.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Ticket 0 committed with payout field = 1 ETH in the Merkle tree.
Step 2: Oracle signs claimWithOracleAuthorization for ticket 0 with payout = 2 ETH.
Step 3: claimedLiability += 2 ETH (if within totalLiability bound).
Step 4: Ticket owner receives 2 ETH instead of the 1 ETH they should get per the Merkle tree.
Step 5: Other winners may be short-changed if total claims approach totalLiability.
preconditions: Oracle is malicious or makes computational errors.
totalLiability has enough room for the inflated payout.

title: MarketFactory.enableMarketRefunds: Can be called by owner to cancel market during Locked phase before settlement timeout -> dos
root_cause: enableMarketRefunds (line 377-381) calls rm.enableRefunds(). enableRefunds (line 473-493) allows cancellation during Locked phase only if block.timestamp >= lockedAt + SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (14 days). This correctly prevents premature cancellation. However, the factory owner controls the oracle (can rotate it) and thus controls whether settlement happens. If the owner intentionally delays settlement for 14 days, they can then cancel the market via enableRefunds, even if settlement was otherwise possible. During this time, users' funds are locked and they cannot claim winnings. The timeout mechanism is meant as an escape hatch but could be weaponized by a malicious owner.
trigger_scenario: Market is locked, result posted, settlement proofs are ready
Malicious factory owner refuses to submit settlement (controls oracle or delays proof submission)
After 14 days (SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS), owner calls enableMarketRefunds
Market is cancelled, users get refunds at face value (ticketSize) instead of potential winnings
Users who would have won more than ticketSize lose their expected profit
preconditions: Market is locked with result posted
Factory owner intentionally delays settlement for 14+ days
Users would have been net winners

title: Verifier.verifyProof: Signal value >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD returns false without revert -> Malformed signals silently rejected
root_cause: In verifyProof (lines 106-110 of Verifier.sol), if any public signal is >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD, the function returns false without reverting. RevealMarket then reverts with InvalidProof. An attacker cannot exploit this to bypass verification because the false return triggers a revert upstream. However, there is a subtle concern: the on-chain signal checks in RevealMarket (e.g., signals[0] == batchRoots[batchIndex]) happen BEFORE the verifier call. If a signal value >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD happens to pass those checks due to wrapping or type casting, the verifier would return false and settlement would fail. Since batchRoots are bytes32 (full 256-bit), a value >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD could match a batch root. But the ZK proof would be invalid for such a value, so the verifier correctly rejects it.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Oracle locks batch roots including a root value >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD.
Step 2: Oracle constructs signals with signals[0] = that root value.
Step 3: On-chain check signals[0] == batchRoots[i] passes.
Step 4: Verifier checks signal >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD, returns false.
Step 5: RevealMarket reverts with InvalidProof. Settlement blocked.
preconditions: Batch root hash value >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD (probability ~18.5% for random hash)

title: ProtocolPool.draw: Unreserved draw path allows draws without prior reservation check -> fund_loss
root_cause: The `draw()` function (line 151-184) has two paths: with reservation (reserved != 0) and without (reserved == 0). In the without-reservation path (line 163-168), the draw succeeds if `amount <= balance - reservedTotal`. This path is only blocked by `drawsPaused` or `marketDrawPaused[market]` flags. A market that never called `reserveLiability` can still draw from idle balance, bypassing the reservation system entirely. While this is intended for legacy/simple markets, it means idle LP capital can be drawn without the LP lock providing any protection since no reservation reduced idle liquidity.
trigger_scenario: LP deposits 100 tokens. Pool: 100 balance, 0 reservedTotal.
Market A is registered with a high liabilityCap but never calls reserveLiability.
Market A calls draw(marketA, 80) without any reservation.
Check passes: reserved == 0, amount(80) <= balance(100) - reservedTotal(0).
80 tokens transferred out. Pool: 20 balance, 100 shares. LP value drops to 0.2 per share.
LP had no warning since idleLiquidity showed 100 (no reservations were made).
preconditions: Market is registered and allowed
Market does not call reserveLiability before draw
drawsPaused is false and marketDrawPaused[market] is false
Sufficient idle balance exists

title: RevealMarket.sweepCancelledRefunds: After refund deadline, unclaimed refund tokens are swept to protocolPool, permanently losing funds for users who didn't refund
root_cause: sweepCancelledRefunds (line 807-819) transfers the entire remaining token balance to protocolPool after the refund deadline (180 days). Any ticket holders who did not call refund/refundSelf/refundTicket before the deadline lose their funds. This is by design (similar to sweepUnclaimed for Settled markets), but the 180-day window should be sufficient for users to claim. The permissionless refundTicket path mitigates this since anyone can trigger refunds for any ticket. However, if refundTicket is not called by anyone (e.g., nobody monitors the cancelled market), the funds are lost after sweep.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market is cancelled with 10 tickets. 7 are refunded via refundTicket.
Step 2: 3 tickets remain unclaimed after refundDeadline.
Step 3: Factory owner calls sweepCancelledRefunds, transferring remaining 3 * ticketSize to protocolPool.
Step 4: Owners of the 3 tickets lose their refunds permanently.
preconditions: Market is in Cancelled phase.
Refund deadline has passed.
Some tickets were not refunded.

title: MarketFactory.updateOracle: Oracle rotation during Commit phase enables malicious oracle injection before lock -> fund_loss
root_cause: RevealMarket.setOracle (line 642-647) allows oracle rotation when phase is Commit or Cancelled. The factory's updateOracle (line 258-263) has no additional phase restrictions. A compromised factory owner can rotate the oracle to a colluding address right before the commit deadline. The malicious oracle can then call lockBatches with fabricated batch roots (that don't match real commitments), post a fraudulent result, and submit fake proofs. However, lockBatches also requires a valid relayerSig from RelayerEscrow.owner(), adding a second check. The attack requires either compromising both oracle and relayer owner, or the owner rotating both.
trigger_scenario: Market is in Commit phase with user commitments and approaching deadline
Compromised factory owner calls updateOracle(market, maliciousOracle)
Commit deadline passes
Malicious oracle calls lockBatches — but this requires a valid relayerSig from relayerEscrow.owner()
If relayer owner is also compromised, lockBatches succeeds with fabricated roots
Malicious oracle calls postResult and verifyAndSettle with forged data
preconditions: Factory owner key is compromised
Relayer owner key is also compromised (lockBatches requires relayer signature)
Market is in Commit phase with user deposits

title: MarketFactory.syncMarketRake: setRakeBps on market reverts if commitments exist, causing unexpected revert for factory owner -> dos
root_cause: RevealMarket.setRakeBps (line 626-631) requires phase == Commit AND commitments.length == 0 (RakeLocked). The factory's syncMarketRake and setMarketRake (lines 230-241) do not check these conditions before calling. If any commitments have been made, the call to rm.setRakeBps will revert with RakeLocked, causing the factory transaction to revert. This is by design (rake cannot change after commitments), but the factory functions don't surface this to the owner clearly — the revert bubbles up from the market.
trigger_scenario: Factory owner updates globalRakeBps to a new value
