Owner calls syncMarketRake(market) to push the new rake to existing markets
Market has at least one commitment — rm.setRakeBps reverts with RakeLocked
syncMarketRake transaction reverts — owner cannot sync rake for this market
This is expected behavior but could confuse the owner when batch-syncing many markets
preconditions: Market has at least one commitment
Factory owner tries to sync or set rake

title: MarketFactory.isVerifierCurrentlyApproved: Verifier key rotation between lock and settle could be detected and blocked, but refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash provides an escape hatch -> Key rotation safety
root_cause: Both verifyAndSettle (line 401) and verifyAndSettleBatched (line 427) check `IVerifier(verifier).verifyingKeyHash() != lockedVerifierKeyHash`. If the verifier owner rotates the key between lock and settle, this check fails. The factory provides `refreshMarketLockedVerifierKey` (MarketFactory line 317-323) which calls `market.refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash()` (RevealMarket line 678-683). However, refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash at line 682 ALSO checks `verifyingKeyHash() != lockedVerifierKeyHash` -- it reverts if they differ! This means `refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash` can only succeed when the key HASN'T changed (it's a no-op assertion). The factory's _validateVerifier also checks `verifyingKeyHash() != approvedVerifierKeyHash[verifier]` (MarketFactory line 530), which pins to the originally approved key hash. So if the verifier key is rotated, both settlement and refresh will fail, effectively bricking the market until the key is rotated BACK to the original. This is safe behavior -- it prevents settlement with unauthorized keys.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market is locked with lockedVerifierKeyHash = H1.
Step 2: Verifier owner rotates the verifying key. New verifyingKeyHash = H2.
Step 3: Oracle tries to settle. verifyingKeyHash() (H2) != lockedVerifierKeyHash (H1). Reverts with VerifierKeyMismatch.
Step 4: Factory owner tries to refresh: refreshLockedVerifierKeyHash also checks H2 != H1. Reverts with VerifierKeyMismatch.
Step 5: Factory owner also cannot re-approve the verifier because pinnedVerifierKeyHash != new keyHash. Reverts with VerifierDrift.
Step 6: Market is stuck in Locked phase until SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS passes and enableRefunds is called.
preconditions: Verifier owner rotates the key after a market is locked

title: ProtocolPool: LOCK_DURATION of 60 days may be insufficient to prevent LP sandwich around known settlement schedules -> unfair_treatment
root_cause: The 60-day lock prevents immediate sandwich attacks. However, if a sophisticated attacker knows a market will settle (and draw from pool) more than 60 days in the future, they can deposit, wait for the lock to expire, and then withdraw immediately before the draw. The commit deadline and settlement timeline are public. If commit deadline is 90 days away at time of deposit, the attacker's lock expires 30 days before the deadline, giving them time to withdraw before any draw occurs. The lock only protects against draws that happen within 60 days of deposit.
trigger_scenario: Market is created with commitDeadline 120 days from now.
Attacker deposits into pool at day 0. Lock expires at day 60.
At day 60, no market draws have occurred (market still in Commit phase).
Attacker withdraws at day 60 with full principal.
Market eventually locks and draws at day 121+. Remaining LPs bear the loss.
Attacker earned yield from the idle balance being available for reservations without bearing settlement risk.
preconditions: Market settlement occurs more than LOCK_DURATION (60 days) after LP deposit
Attacker can time deposits relative to market schedules
Pool has no external yield mechanism (LPs don't profit from idle balance)

title: RevealMarket._computeLeaf: salt parameter as bytes32 can exceed SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD, causing FieldElementOutOfRange revert and blocking legitimate claims
root_cause: _computeLeaf checks uint256(salt) >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD at line 864. The salt is a bytes32 which when cast to uint256 can be any 256-bit value. If a user's commitment was generated with a salt whose uint256 representation >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD (the BN254 scalar field is ~254 bits, so ~1/4 of all possible bytes32 values exceed it), the claim will revert with FieldElementOutOfRange. However, PoseidonT3.poseidon reduces inputs via modular arithmetic (state[1] = inputs[0] % PRIME at line 13), meaning the commitment was stored using the reduced value. The on-chain claim tries to compute the leaf with the unreduced value but hits the range check first. The user would need to provide salt % SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD to claim, but the original salt was used for the commitment during commit phase. Actually, examining commitWithAuthorization, the commitment is opaque bytes32 passed in auth.commitment — it is pre-computed off-chain. So the off-chain system must ensure salt < SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD. If the off-chain system uses unreduced salts, commitments may be stored that can never be claimed.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Off-chain system generates a random bytes32 salt where uint256(salt) >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD.
Step 2: Off-chain system computes the Poseidon leaf using Poseidon library that automatically reduces mod PRIME.
Step 3: Commitment is stored on-chain via commitWithAuthorization (no validation of salt value).
Step 4: Market settles. User tries to claim with the original salt.
Step 5: _computeLeaf reverts with FieldElementOutOfRange because uint256(salt) >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD.

Step 6: User cannot claim. Even if they try salt % SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD, the resulting leaf will differ from what's stored (since the Poseidon lib already reduced in the off-chain computation but the nesting order may differ).
preconditions: Off-chain commitment generation uses salt values that are not checked against SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD.
Salt is randomly generated as full 256-bit value.

title: MarketFactory.setVerifierApproval: Proxy verifier bypasses codehash pinning -> theft_of_yield
root_cause: setVerifierApproval pins verifier.codehash on first approval (line 182-190). If the verifier is deployed behind a transparent or UUPS proxy, the codehash is the proxy's codehash which never changes even when the implementation is upgraded. The pinned codehash check (line 188) would pass even after the implementation logic is silently swapped. The verifyingKeyHash and circuitHash are read from the verifier via external calls, so a compromised implementation could return the expected values while actually accepting forged proofs. However, Verifier.sol is Ownable2Step with renounceOwnership disabled and uses no proxy pattern, so this risk requires intentional deployment of a proxy verifier.
trigger_scenario: Owner deploys a verifier behind a minimal proxy (ERC1967 or similar) where the proxy codehash is stable
Owner calls setVerifierApproval(proxyVerifier, true) — proxy codehash and initial keyHash are pinned
Owner (or compromised owner) upgrades the proxy implementation to a malicious verifier that returns true for any proof
Malicious implementation returns identical circuitHash(), verifyingKeyHash(), expectedInputs() values
isVerifierCurrentlyApproved passes all checks since proxy codehash hasn't changed
Oracle calls verifyAndSettle with a forged proof that the malicious implementation accepts
preconditions: Verifier is deployed behind a proxy contract (not the standard Verifier.sol)
Owner controls both the factory and the proxy admin
A market is in Locked phase with active escrow

title: RevealMarket.lockBatches: Batch roots not validated against on-chain commitments -> Oracle can lock arbitrary roots
root_cause: lockBatches (lines 325-378) validates that the number of batches matches `ceil(commitments.length / BATCH_SIZE)` and that each batch count matches the expected size. However, it does NOT verify that the provided `roots[]` are actually the Poseidon Merkle roots of the stored `commitments[]`. The roots are taken at face value from the oracle's calldata. The on-chain contract stores individual commitments (line 310: `commitments.push(auth.commitment)`) but never builds the Merkle tree on-chain. The relayer signature attests to the roots, providing a second trust anchor. But if both oracle and relayer owner collude (or if the relayer owner blindly signs), arbitrary roots could be locked, enabling settlement proofs that don't correspond to actual user commitments.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Users commit tickets; commitments[] stores their Poseidon leaf hashes.
Step 2: Oracle computes fake roots that include a different set of leaves (e.g., all payouts going to attacker-controlled addresses).
Step 3: Oracle obtains relayer signature on the fake roots (relayer owner doesn't independently verify).
Step 4: Oracle calls lockBatches with fake roots. On-chain validation passes (counts match, roots.length matches).
Step 5: Oracle generates ZK proofs against fake roots, settles market.
Step 6: Claims using real commitments fail _verifyLeaf because the Merkle proof won't match the fake roots.
Step 7: Attacker can claim with the fake leaf data.
preconditions: Oracle must be malicious or compromised
Relayer owner must sign the fake roots (colluding or not independently verifying)
Attacker must be able to generate valid Groth16 proofs for the fake tree

title: ProtocolPool.reserveLiability: Reservation can lock up pool liquidity for up to SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS + processing time -> LP liquidity DoS
root_cause: When lockBatches calls `protocolPool.reserveLiability(address(this), protocolLiabilityCap)` (RevealMarket line 373), the pool's `reservedTotal` increases by `protocolLiabilityCap`. This reduces available idle liquidity for LP withdrawals (`idle = balance - reservedTotal` in ProtocolPool line 253). The reservation is released in `_finalizeSettlement` (line 749) or `enableRefunds` (line 492). If settlement takes the full SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (14 days) before refunds are enabled, LP funds are locked for that duration plus the LOCK_DURATION. If many markets are locked simultaneously, all their reservations stack, potentially locking all pool liquidity. This is by design but could griefing LPs who want to withdraw.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Pool has 1000 ETH from LPs.
Step 2: 10 markets are created, each with protocolLiabilityCap = 100 ETH.
Step 3: All 10 markets are locked. reservedTotal = 1000 ETH.
Step 4: idle = 1000 - 1000 = 0. LPs cannot withdraw.
Step 5: Markets take 14 days to settle or timeout. LPs are locked out for that period.
preconditions: Multiple markets locked simultaneously
Combined protocolLiabilityCap >= pool balance

title: ProtocolPool.lpWithdraw: Rounding in _lpShareValue underwater causes LP to receive 0 for small share amounts -> griefing
root_cause: When pool is severely underwater, `_lpShareValue` computes `Math.mulDiv(shares, totalAssets(), totalShares)`. If `shares * totalAssets < totalShares`, the result rounds down to 0. The `lpWithdraw` function checks `if (assets == 0) revert InvalidAmount()` on line 249. So an LP trying to redeem a small number of shares when the pool is very underwater gets reverted. They cannot redeem small amounts, but they can still redeem larger amounts. This could prevent incremental withdrawals but is not a fund lock since a larger redemption would work.
trigger_scenario: Pool: 1 wei asset, 1000e18 shares (extremely underwater).
LP tries to redeem 1 share: _lpShareValue(1) = mulDiv(1, 1, 1000e18) = 0.
lpWithdraw reverts with InvalidAmount.
LP must redeem at least 1000e18 shares to get 1 wei. Practically all shares at once.
Not a critical issue but prevents granular withdrawal.
preconditions: Pool is severely underwater
LP tries to redeem a small number of shares

title: RevealMarket.setClaimsPaused: Pausing claims during Settled phase correctly tracks pause duration but allows the factory owner to indefinitely block claims
root_cause: setClaimsPaused(true) blocks all claims (line 455: if (claimsPaused) revert ClaimsPaused()). While the pause extends the effective deadline (so users don't lose their claim window), the factory owner can keep claims paused indefinitely. There is no maximum pause duration or governance timelock. This is a centralization risk: a malicious or compromised factory owner can prevent all users from claiming their legitimate winnings, and then sweep the funds after the effective deadline eventually passes (though the deadline extends while paused, so sweep also cannot execute during pause). The factory owner would need to unpause, let the deadline pass quickly if enough pause duration was accumulated, then sweep. Actually, since _effectiveClaimDeadline adds pause duration, and sweepUnclaimed checks block.timestamp > _effectiveClaimDeadline(), the effective deadline is extended by all pause time. So the factory owner would need to let the remaining claim window elapse after unpausing.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market settles. Claims begin.
Step 2: Factory owner calls setClaimsPaused(true). Claims blocked.
Step 3: 365 days pass while paused. claimPauseTotalDuration accumulates.
Step 4: Factory owner calls setClaimsPaused(false). Claims resume.
Step 5: The effective claim deadline is now 180 days (original) + 365 days (pause) = 545 days from settlement.
Step 6: Users must still claim within 180 days of unpausing (the remaining window). If they missed the announcement, funds could be swept.
preconditions: Factory owner pauses claims for extended period.
Users are not monitoring for unpause events.

title: MarketFactory.setRelayerCommitsPaused: try/catch silently skips failed relayers -> dos
root_cause: _setRelayerCommitsPausedBatch (line 541-562) iterates activeRelayers and calls setCommitsPaused on each with try/catch. If a relayer's setCommitsPaused reverts (e.g., relayer contract is self-destructed, or its setCommitsPaused has a bug), the failure is silently caught and only an event RelayerPausePropagationFailed is emitted. The function continues to the next relayer. This means an emergency pause might not reach all relayers, leaving some relayers still accepting commits while the factory owner believes all are paused. Additionally, the function reads back commitsPaused() to verify (line 551) but failures there are also caught silently.
trigger_scenario: Factory owner detects a critical vulnerability and calls setRelayerCommitsPaused(true)
RelayerEscrow R1 is paused successfully
RelayerEscrow R2 has been upgraded/self-destructed/has a bug — setCommitsPaused reverts
try/catch catches the revert, emits RelayerPausePropagationFailed(R2)
Function continues, R3 is paused successfully
R2 remains unpaused — users can still commit through R2 during the supposed emergency stop
preconditions: At least one relayer in activeRelayers has a malfunctioning setCommitsPaused
Factory owner initiates an emergency pause

title: MarketFactory.isVerifierCurrentlyApproved: External calls to compromised verifier return attacker-controlled values -> fund_loss
root_cause: isVerifierCurrentlyApproved (line 207-220) makes multiple external calls to the verifier contract: owner(), expectedInputs(), circuitHash(), verifyingKeyHash(). If the verifier contract is compromised (e.g., via a proxy upgrade or SELFDESTRUCT+CREATE2 redeployment), these calls could return crafted values that pass all checks while the actual verifyProof logic accepts forged proofs. The codehash check (line 215) mitigates SELFDESTRUCT+redeploy since the new code would have a different hash. However, a proxy-based verifier would retain the same codehash while the implementation could be swapped. The Verifier.sol contract does not use a proxy pattern and has renounceOwnership disabled, but the factory does not enforce that verifiers must not be proxies.
trigger_scenario: A verifier is deployed behind an upgradeable proxy and approved by the factory owner
Proxy codehash is pinned on first approval
Attacker (or compromised owner) upgrades the proxy implementation
New implementation returns valid-looking owner(), expectedInputs(), circuitHash(), verifyingKeyHash()
But verifyProof() in the new implementation always returns true
isVerifierCurrentlyApproved returns true, and settlement proceeds with forged proofs
preconditions: Verifier is deployed as an upgradeable proxy (not enforced against by the factory)
Proxy admin key is compromised or owner is malicious
Market is in Locked phase awaiting settlement

title: RevealMarket.setClaimsPaused: Pausing claims after settlement extends effective claim deadline indefinitely -> unfair_treatment
root_cause: setClaimsPaused (line 699-711) tracks pause durations when phase == Settled. When claims are paused, claimPauseStartedAt is set to block.timestamp. _effectiveClaimDeadline (line 906-912) adds claimPauseTotalDuration plus the current ongoing pause duration. If the factory owner pauses claims and never unpauses, the effective claim deadline extends indefinitely (it keeps growing with block.timestamp). This means sweepUnclaimed can never be called (it requires block.timestamp > effectiveClaimDeadline). Funds remain locked in the market contract forever. The factory owner must unpause claims to allow the claim window to eventually close.
trigger_scenario: Market settles, claim deadline is set to block.timestamp + 180 days
Factory owner calls setMarketClaimsPaused(market, true) for emergency review
Owner loses access to key or forgets to unpause
Effective claim deadline keeps extending: claimDeadline + (block.timestamp - claimPauseStartedAt)
sweepUnclaimed always reverts with ClaimWindowOpen
Unclaimed funds are permanently locked unless owner unpauses or a new owner is set via Ownable2Step
preconditions: Market is in Settled phase
Claims are paused and never unpaused
Owner key is lost or unavailable

title: RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization: Rake rounding to zero for small ticketSize allows zero-rake commits -> protocol revenue loss
root_cause: The rake calculation at line 312 is: rake = (ticketSize * rakeBps) / 10_000. For small ticketSize values, this rounds down to zero. For example: ticketSize=99, rakeBps=100 -> rake = (99 * 100) / 10_000 = 9900 / 10_000 = 0. The net amount equals the full ticketSize. This means the protocol collects zero rake on these commits. While ticketSize is set once at initialization and typically represents a meaningful amount (e.g., 1 USDC = 1e6), if a market were configured with a very small ticketSize (< 100 base units), the rake could be systematically zero.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market is initialized with ticketSize = 99 (smallest unit), rakeBps = 100 (1%).
Step 2: User commits. rake = (99 * 100) / 10_000 = 0.
Step 3: net = ticketSize - 0 = 99. totalEscrow += 99, rakeCollected += 0.
Step 4: Protocol collects no rake despite rakeBps being set to 1%.
preconditions: ticketSize * rakeBps < 10_000
Market initialized with small ticketSize

title: RevealMarket.lockBatches: Relayer signature does not commit to commitDeadline or totalEscrow -> Signature reuse across scenarios
root_cause: The relayer signature in lockBatches (lines 336-343) signs over `(address(this), factory, marketId, roots, counts, block.chainid)`. It does NOT include `totalEscrow`, `commitDeadline`, `commitments.length`, or `block.timestamp`. While the roots and counts are deterministic from the commitment data, the signature could theoretically be reused if the oracle calls lockBatches at different times producing the same roots/counts (e.g., if commitments happen to be identical). In practice, commitments are Poseidon hashes including unique ticket IDs and salts, so identical roots are astronomically unlikely. The bigger concern is that the relayer owner signs the roots before actually verifying them -- the signature attests agreement with the batch decomposition, but the relayer owner has no way to independently verify the Poseidon Merkle roots on-chain.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Oracle computes batch Merkle roots off-chain and requests relayer owner's signature.
Step 2: Relayer owner signs without independently verifying the roots (trusts oracle).
Step 3: Oracle provides malicious roots that don't match the actual commitments.
Step 4: lockBatches succeeds because the on-chain code does not verify roots against stored commitments.
Step 5: During settlement, proofs are verified against the malicious roots, and any valid proof for those roots would succeed.
preconditions: Oracle and relayer owner must not independently verify Merkle roots off-chain
Oracle must be malicious or compromised

title: RevealMarket.enableRefunds: Settlement timeout of 14 days may be too short if oracle is temporarily unavailable, leading to premature cancellation
root_cause: SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 14 days (line 38). After lockBatches, if 14 days pass without full settlement, any caller of enableRefunds (via factory) can cancel the market. This is a safety mechanism to prevent indefinite lockup. However, 14 days may be insufficient if: (a) the oracle is temporarily offline, (b) the ZK prover is backlogged, or (c) network congestion delays settlement transactions. Once cancelled, the market cannot be settled — all users get refunds instead of payouts. Winners lose their expected profits. The factory owner controls enableRefunds, so premature cancellation requires factory owner action.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market locks at time T.
Step 2: Oracle service goes down for 15 days.
Step 3: Factory owner calls enableRefunds at T + 15 days. lockedAt + 14 days < block.timestamp.
Step 4: Market is cancelled. Winners who would have received payouts now only get ticketSize refund.
Step 5: If the oracle comes back at T + 16 days, settlement is no longer possible.
preconditions: Market is in Locked phase.
14 days have elapsed since locking.
Factory owner decides to cancel.

title: MarketFactory.updateProtocolLiabilityCap: Cap update on market and pool is not atomic with respect to reservation state -> protocol_insolvency
root_cause: updateProtocolLiabilityCap (line 341-347) calls rm.setProtocolLiabilityCap(newCap) then pool.updateLiabilityCap(market, newCap). The market's setProtocolLiabilityCap requires phase == Commit (line 688), which means no reservation has been taken yet (reservations happen at lockBatches). The pool's updateLiabilityCap checks newCap >= consumedLiability + reservedLiability (line 106), but since phase is Commit, reservedLiability should be 0. This is safe. However, if the cap is increased to a very large value, and the market is later locked with a large protocolLiabilityCap, the pool might not have enough funds to cover the reservation. reserveLiability does check balance >= reservedTotal + amount (line 122), so this would revert at lock time. No insolvency risk.
trigger_scenario: Factory owner sets protocolLiabilityCap to a very large value for market M
Market M enters commit phase and fills up with commitments
Oracle calls lockBatches — reserveLiability is called with protocolLiabilityCap amount
If pool balance < reservedTotal + protocolLiabilityCap, reserveLiability reverts with InsufficientPool
Lock fails, market cannot proceed to settlement
Users must wait for enableRefunds after the commit deadline + settlement timeout
preconditions: protocolLiabilityCap is set larger than pool can cover
Market fills with commitments

title: RelayerEscrow.setCommitsPaused: Both owner and marketFactory can pause, creating potential conflicting state -> dos
root_cause: RelayerEscrow.setCommitsPaused (line 175-179) allows both owner() and marketFactory to set the commitsPaused flag. If the factory pauses the relayer and the relayer owner unpauses it (or vice versa), they can enter a toggle war. The last caller wins. This is by design — both entities should have emergency pause capability. However, it means the factory's setRelayerCommitsPaused may be overridden by the relayer owner immediately after. In practice, the relayer owner and factory owner should be coordinating, and in many deployments they may be the same entity.
trigger_scenario: Factory owner calls setRelayerCommitsPaused(true) — all relayers paused
Relayer R1's owner calls R1.setCommitsPaused(false) — R1 is unpaused
Factory believes all relayers are paused, but R1 is accepting commits
This could undermine an emergency pause if relayer owners are not cooperative
preconditions: Factory owner and relayer owner are different entities
They disagree on pause state

title: RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization: commitment value not validated against SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD -> invalid commitment could be stored
root_cause: The commitment (auth.commitment) is a bytes32 value pushed directly into the commitments array. In _computeLeaf (used during claims), field elements are validated against SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD. However, the commitment itself is the output of an off-chain Poseidon hash, which should already be within the field. If the commitment exceeds SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD, the Merkle tree verification during claims would still work (the batch roots are computed off-chain using the same commitments), but the ZK proof verification might fail depending on how the circuit handles out-of-range values. commitWithAuthorization does not validate commitment < SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD. This could allow storing a commitment that is inconsistent with the ZK circuit's field, potentially causing settlement to fail.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Backend signs authorization with commitment = SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD + 1 (a value exceeding the BN254 scalar field).
Step 2: commitWithAuthorization stores this commitment without validation.
Step 3: During lockBatches, the off-chain batch root computation may handle this value differently than the ZK circuit.
Step 4: The Groth16 proof may fail because the public input (batch root) does not match what the circuit expects.
Step 5: Settlement could be permanently blocked for this batch.
preconditions: Backend signer signs a commitment outside the SNARK scalar field

title: RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization: authorizationSigner can be rotated during commit phase -> existing signed-but-unsubmitted authorizations become invalid
root_cause: setAuthorizationSigner can be called by the factory during Phase.Commit to change the authorizationSigner. Any commit authorizations that were signed by the previous signer but not yet submitted on-chain will fail signature verification (digest.recover(signature) != newAuthorizationSigner). This is a griefing vector if the factory rotates the signer while commits are in-flight. The impact is that users who received valid authorizations from the backend must re-request them signed by the new signer. The user's escrow balance is not affected (commitOnBehalf would revert, and the balance deduction would be rolled back).
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Backend signs 100 commit authorizations with signer key A.
Step 2: Factory calls setAuthorizationSigner(signerB). authorizationSigner = signerB.
Step 3: Relayer submits the 100 commits with signatures from signer A.
Step 4: All 100 commits revert with InvalidSignature because the recovered signer is A but authorizationSigner is now B.
Step 5: Backend must re-sign all 100 authorizations with signer B.
preconditions: Factory rotates authorizationSigner during active commit period

title: ProtocolPool.lpWithdraw: First-come-first-served withdrawal creates unfair LP race condition -> unfair_treatment
root_cause: The `lpWithdraw` function checks `assets > idle` where idle = `balance - reservedTotal` (lines 251-254). When the pool is underwater, the first LP to withdraw gets the most favorable payout. After the first withdrawal, remaining LPs face a worse ratio because total assets decreased but their share count remains. This is demonstrated in the test `testTwoLpsFirstComeFirstServed`. While this is inherent to any pool with shared losses and sequential withdrawals, the lack of a withdrawal queue or pro-rata mechanism means LPs who withdraw first externalize more loss to later LPs.
trigger_scenario: LP1 and LP2 each have 100 unlocked shares. Pool: 120 assets, 200 shares (underwater after draw).
LP1 withdraws 100 shares: gets 100 * 120/200 = 60 tokens. Pool: 60 assets, 100 shares.
LP2 withdraws 100 shares: gets 100 * 60/100 = 60 tokens. Pool: 0 assets, 0 shares.
Both get 60 — fair in this case. But if LP1 only withdraws 50 shares:
LP1 gets 50 * 120/200 = 30. Pool: 90 assets, 150 shares.
LP2 withdraws 100: gets 100 * 90/150 = 60. LP1 later gets 50 * 30/50 = 30.
Same outcome. The math actually distributes proportionally. This is safe.
preconditions: Pool is underwater
Multiple LPs with unlocked shares
Sequential withdrawal execution

title: ProtocolPool: Market settlement returns surplus directly to pool, inflating balance but not crediting LPs -> theft_of_yield
root_cause: After market settlement, `_finalizeSettlement` in RevealMarket transfers surplus back to the protocol pool via `_safeTransferExact(protocolPool, surplus)` (RevealMarket line 738). This increases pool's `balanceOf` but doesn't mint any LP shares. The surplus accrues to `protocolSurplus()` (balance - totalShares), not to LP share value (capped at 1:1). This is explicitly by design: LPs bear losses but don't profit from surplus. The surplus goes to the protocol owner. While this is documented, it means LPs take asymmetric risk: unlimited downside from draws, zero upside from surplus.
trigger_scenario: LP deposits 100. Market draws 50 (LP value = 0.5).
Market settles favorably. 80 surplus returned to pool. Pool: 130 assets, 100 shares.
LP value = min(100 * 130/100, 100) = 100. LP recovered to principal.
30 surplus (130 - 100) goes to protocol owner, not LP.
LP bore the risk of the 50 draw but gets no upside from the 80 surplus.
preconditions: Market settlement produces surplus
LP deposits existed during the draw period

title: RevealMarket.claim: claimedLiability accumulation allows legitimate claims to fail with OverClaimed if ZK circuit computes totalLiability incorrectly
root_cause: In _finalizeSettlement (line 717), totalLiability is set from the ZK proof's public signals (publicSignals[4]). If the ZK circuit computes a totalLiability that is less than the sum of all individual winning ticket payouts, then after some claims succeed, subsequent legitimate claims will revert with OverClaimed (line 466: if (claimedLiability > totalLiability) revert OverClaimed()). The contract trusts the ZK proof output for totalLiability, and the invariant poolYes + poolNo == totalLiability is checked (line 716), but there is no separate check that totalLiability >= sum of all individual payouts. This is a circuit-level trust assumption.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market has 10 winning tickets, each with payout of 1 ETH, total should be 10 ETH.
Step 2: ZK circuit computes totalLiability = 9 ETH due to a bug (e.g., off-by-one in padding).
Step 3: Settlement succeeds because the circuit proof verifies and poolYes + poolNo == 9 ETH.
Step 4: First 9 claims succeed (claimedLiability = 9 ETH).
Step 5: 10th claim reverts with OverClaimed because claimedLiability + 1 > 9.
preconditions: ZK circuit has a bug that computes totalLiability less than the actual sum of winning payouts.
Verifier accepts the proof (depends on circuit correctness).

title: RevealMarket._computeLeaf: Poseidon hash nesting order (h1=[ticketId,outcomeId], h2=[amount,payout], h3=[h2,userSalt], leaf=[h1,h3]) must match off-chain exactly or claims fail
root_cause: _computeLeaf uses a specific 4-level Poseidon nesting: userSalt=Poseidon(uint160(user), salt), h1=Poseidon(ticketId, outcomeId), h2=Poseidon(amount, payout), h3=Poseidon(h2, userSalt), leaf=Poseidon(h1, h3). If the off-chain prover or commitment generator uses a different nesting order (e.g., swapping left/right inputs in any Poseidon call), the resulting leaf will be different, and on-chain claims will fail with InvalidMerkleProof. This is a correctness concern for the off-chain integration, not a smart contract vulnerability per se. The PoseidonTestUtils in the test suite mirrors this exact ordering (line 24-29 of PoseidonTestUtils.sol), confirming the canonical order. Any off-chain implementation must follow this exact ordering.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Off-chain system computes leaf using Poseidon(outcomeId, ticketId) instead of Poseidon(ticketId, outcomeId).
Step 2: Commitment is stored on-chain.
Step 3: Market settles. User tries to claim.
Step 4: On-chain _computeLeaf produces different hash than stored commitment.
Step 5: commitments[ticketId] != leaf, _verifyLeaf returns false.
Step 6: Claim reverts with InvalidMerkleProof. User must use claimWithOracleAuthorization as fallback.
preconditions: Off-chain Poseidon implementation uses different argument ordering.
Commitment was stored with the mismatched hash.

title: RelayerEscrow.setMarketFactory: Factory lock only prevents change to different non-zero address -> loss_of_function
root_cause: RelayerEscrow.setMarketFactory (line 65-69) checks if(marketFactory != address(0) && marketFactory != factory) revert FactoryLocked. This means: (a) first call with any non-zero address succeeds, (b) subsequent calls with the SAME address succeed (no-op), (c) subsequent calls with a DIFFERENT address revert. This correctly locks the factory to the first non-zero value. However, the first setMarketFactory call is critical — if the relayer owner accidentally sets it to the wrong factory, it cannot be corrected. This is a one-shot configuration with no recovery path.
trigger_scenario: Relayer owner calls setMarketFactory with an incorrect factory address
The factory is locked to the wrong address
No legitimate factory can register markets with this relayer
Relayer becomes unusable — must deploy a new RelayerEscrow
If users already deposited, their funds are safe (they can withdraw) but the relayer cannot participate in markets
preconditions: Relayer owner sets marketFactory to wrong address on first call
Users may have already deposited into the relayer

title: MarketFactory.updateMarketProtocolPool: Old pool's market registration and reservation are not cleaned up -> protocol_insolvency
root_cause: updateMarketProtocolPool (line 326-338) registers the market on the new pool and calls rm.setProtocolPool, but does NOT unregister the market from the old pool. The guard (line 333) ensures phase == Commit and nextTicketId == 0, meaning no reservation has been taken on the old pool. However, allowedMarket[market] remains true on the old pool. Since the market's protocolPool address is updated to the new pool, all future interactions (reserveLiability, draw, releaseLiabilityReservation) will go to the new pool. The old pool's stale allowedMarket entry has no functional impact since the market would call the new pool, not the old one. The market address could theoretically call old pool functions directly, but the market only calls its stored protocolPool address.
trigger_scenario: Market M is created with ProtocolPool P1, registered on P1
Factory owner rotates to P2: registerMarket(M) on P2, setProtocolPool(P2) on M
P1.allowedMarket[M] remains true, P1.liabilityCap[M] retains old value
M.protocolPool is now P2 — all subsequent calls go to P2
Stale state on P1 is bookkeeping noise but no funds are at risk
If someone deploys a contract at M's address on a different chain (irrelevant for same-chain)
preconditions: Market's protocol pool is rotated
Phase is Commit with no tickets

title: RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization: ticketId validation prevents gaps but commitment array is append-only -> no ticket ID manipulation
root_cause: Line 286-287 enforce: expectedTicketId = commitments.length, and auth.ticketId must equal expectedTicketId. This means ticket IDs are strictly sequential (0, 1, 2, ...) and cannot be skipped or reordered. The backend signer must include the correct ticketId in the authorization. If two commits are submitted concurrently, one will succeed (incrementing the length) and the other will revert because its ticketId no longer matches commitments.length. This is correct behavior -- it serializes commits and prevents ID manipulation. The relayer must coordinate sequential submissions.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: commitments.length = 5. Backend signs auth with ticketId=5.
Step 2: Commit succeeds. commitments.length = 6.
Step 3: Another commit was signed for ticketId=5 (race condition). It reverts with TicketIndexMismatch.
Step 4: Backend must re-sign with ticketId=6 for the second commit.
preconditions: Concurrent commit attempts

title: Verifier._pairingCheck: Gas-limited external self-call returns false instead of reverting -> Malicious proof accepted as invalid rather than causing revert
root_cause: The Verifier uses `this._pairingCheck(proof, vkx)` wrapped in a try/catch (line 122-126 of Verifier.sol). The _pairingCheck function calls the bn128 pairing precompile (address 0x08) via staticcall. If the pairing precompile runs out of gas, the staticcall returns false (not revert), which propagates up through the `require(success, ...)` as a revert. The try/catch in verifyProof then catches this and returns `false`. This means gas manipulation cannot cause a valid proof to be silently rejected as invalid -- the caller (RevealMarket) will revert with `InvalidProof`, not settle with wrong data. However, this is a defense-in-depth concern: the `false` return path means no funds are at risk; the market simply cannot settle until a properly-gassed call is made.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Oracle submits verifyAndSettle or verifyAndSettleBatched with a valid proof but with carefully calculated gas that is sufficient to reach the _pairingCheck but insufficient for the precompile to execute.
Step 2: The pairing precompile staticcall fails due to insufficient gas, `require(success)` reverts inside _pairingCheck.
Step 3: The try/catch in verifyProof catches the revert and returns false.
Step 4: RevealMarket reverts with InvalidProof, preventing settlement.
preconditions: Oracle or gas-manipulating relayer can control the gas forwarded to the verifier call

title: RevealMarket.lockBatches: Poseidon Merkle root as bytes32 may exceed SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD -> Unsettleable market
root_cause: Batch roots are stored as bytes32 values and compared to signals[0] as uint256 in _verifyBatchProof (line 831: `signals[0] != uint256(batchRoots[batchIndex])`). The Verifier checks `signal >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD` and returns false if any signal exceeds the field. The SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD is approximately 2^254, so about 6.25% of the uint256 space exceeds it. However, Poseidon hash outputs are inherently within the BN254 scalar field because Poseidon operates over that field. So Poseidon-based Merkle roots should always be < SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD. The risk only exists if the off-chain computation produces incorrect roots or if a non-Poseidon hash is used. The contract does not validate that roots are < SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD in lockBatches.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Off-chain root computation has a bug producing a root >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD.
Step 2: Oracle calls lockBatches with this root. No on-chain validation of root range.
Step 3: Oracle attempts settlement with signals[0] = root value.
Step 4: Verifier rejects because signal >= SNARK_SCALAR_FIELD. Returns false.
Step 5: Market is unsettleable. Must wait for SETTLEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS and use enableRefunds.
preconditions: Off-chain Merkle root computation bug producing out-of-field values

title: ProtocolPool.registerMarket: Re-registration resets consumedLiability allowing double draws -> fund_loss
root_cause: The `registerMarket` function (line 95-102) sets `consumedLiability[market] = 0` and `reservedLiability[market] = 0` unconditionally. If a market is re-registered (e.g., factory calls registerMarket again for an existing market), its consumed liability counter is reset to zero. This would allow the market to draw up to its full cap again, even though it already drew from the pool previously. However, the factory's `createMarket` only calls `registerMarket` for newly created markets, and there's no path to re-register. The factory's `updateMarketProtocolPool` registers on the NEW pool, not the old one.
trigger_scenario: Factory creates Market A, which gets registered with pool. liabilityCap = 100.
Market A draws 80 from pool. consumedLiability[A] = 80.
Factory owner calls some path that triggers registerMarket(A, 100) again on same pool.
consumedLiability[A] is reset to 0. Market A can now draw another 100.
But: there is no factory path that re-registers on the same pool. Factory.createMarket creates new markets. Factory.updateMarketProtocolPool registers on a new pool only.
Could occur if marketFactory is set to a malicious address.
preconditions: marketFactory is set to a malicious or buggy factory
The factory calls registerMarket for an already-registered market on the same pool

title: RevealMarket.claim: Winning outcome check ensures only correct outcome tickets are claimable but does not verify ticket amount matches expected payout
root_cause: claim() at line 458 checks outcomeId != winningOutcomeId and reverts with WrongOutcome. This prevents losing tickets from claiming. The payout amount is embedded in the Merkle tree leaf and verified via _verifyLeaf (Poseidon Merkle proof against the batch root). The ZK circuit is responsible for ensuring the payout values in the Merkle tree are correct. If the ZK circuit accepted invalid payout values, they would be baked into the Merkle root, and claims would succeed with those incorrect payouts. The on-chain contract trusts the ZK proof and Merkle root. This is the intended trust model.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: ZK circuit computes payouts incorrectly (e.g., payout for a winning ticket is 2x the correct amount).
Step 2: Merkle root embeds these incorrect payouts.
Step 3: Market settles with the incorrect Merkle root.
Step 4: User claims with the inflated payout. Merkle proof verifies against the (incorrect) root.
Step 5: claimedLiability increases by the inflated amount. Other winners may hit OverClaimed.
preconditions: ZK circuit has a payout computation bug.
Verifier accepts the proof.

title: RevealMarket.setRelayerEscrow: No phase guard allows relayer rotation during Locked/Settled phases -> fund_loss
root_cause: RevealMarket.setRelayerEscrow (line 650-654) has only an onlyFactory modifier with no phase check. The MarketFactory.updateMarketRelayer (line 266-286) enforces phase == Commit && nextTicketId == 0 (line 272), providing indirect protection. However, setRelayerEscrow is a public function that could theoretically be called by any code path in the factory. If a new factory function is added in a future upgrade that calls setRelayerEscrow without the phase guard, or if the factory is redeployed with a different implementation, the relayer could be rotated during Locked or Settled phase. In the current codebase, only updateMarketRelayer calls setRelayerEscrow, so this is safe but fragile.
trigger_scenario: Current code: updateMarketRelayer is the only caller of rm.setRelayerEscrow() — safe
Future upgrade scenario: a new factory function calls rm.setRelayerEscrow() without the phase+ticket guard
Relayer is rotated while market is in Locked phase with active user deposits
New relayer has different user balances, breaking the refund or claim flow
Users who deposited through the old relayer cannot get refunds
preconditions: A new factory code path calls setRelayerEscrow without phase guard (not present in current code)
Market is in Locked or Settled phase with user funds

title: RelayerEscrow: accountedCollateral can desync if market refunds tokens directly to escrow without creditFromMarket -> permanent excess collateral
root_cause: When commitOnBehalf sends ticketSize to a market, it decrements accountedCollateral by ticketSize. If the market later refunds by transferring tokens back to the escrow address (e.g., via safeTransfer(escrow, ticketSize)) without going through creditFromMarket, the tokens arrive but accountedCollateral is not incremented. This creates 'excess collateral' (balanceOf(escrow) > accountedCollateral). The owner can recover this via recoverExcessCollateral. However, the user whose balance was debited for the commit does not get credited back. In practice, RevealMarket refund paths (refundTicket, refund, refundSelf) send tokens directly to the user, not back to the escrow. The creditFromMarket function is designed for escrow-style payouts. If a market were to transfer tokens to the escrow outside of creditFromMarket, the accountedCollateral would be permanently behind, but the excess is recoverable by the owner. The user impact depends on whether the user's balance in the escrow was the relevant accounting.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: User deposits 100 into escrow. balances[user]=100, accountedCollateral=100.
Step 2: commitOnBehalf debits ticketSize=100. balances[user]=0, accountedCollateral=0. Market has 100.
Step 3: Market is cancelled and refundTicket sends 100 directly to the user (not to escrow).
Step 4: accountedCollateral remains 0, escrow token balance is 0. No desync.
Step 5: If instead the market sends 100 back to the escrow via raw transfer, escrow balance=100, accountedCollateral=0. Excess=100 that owner can recover, but user's balance is still 0.
preconditions: Market transfers tokens to escrow address outside of creditFromMarket

title: RevealMarket.lockBatches: Relayer signature validation uses RelayerEscrow owner which can change -> Signature from old owner still valid if owner hasn't changed
root_cause: lockBatches (line 342) reads the current `RelayerEscrow(payable(relayerEscrow)).owner()` to validate the relayer signature. RelayerEscrow inherits Ownable2Step, so ownership transfers require a two-step process. If the relayer owner is transferred between when the signature was obtained and when lockBatches is called, the signature would be invalid (signed by old owner, validated against new owner). This is a standard operational concern, not a vulnerability -- the oracle would simply need to get a new signature from the new owner. Conversely, if an attacker obtains a signature from the current owner and ownership is NOT transferred, the signature remains valid indefinitely (no expiry in the signed data). However, the signed data includes the specific roots and counts, so it's only valid for that exact batch decomposition.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Relayer owner signs roots/counts for a market.
Step 2: Before oracle calls lockBatches, relayer ownership is transferred via Ownable2Step.
Step 3: lockBatches validates signature against new owner. Signature check fails with InvalidRelayerSignature.
Step 4: Oracle must obtain a new signature from the new owner.
preconditions: Relayer ownership must be transferred between signature creation and lockBatches call

title: RevealMarket._finalizeSettlement: poolYes + poolNo == totalLiability invariant ensures correct liability accounting but doesn't prevent individual payout inflation
root_cause: _finalizeSettlement checks poolYes_ + poolNo_ != totalLiability_ at line 716 and reverts with SettlementInvariantMismatch. This ensures the total yes and no side payouts sum to totalLiability. However, this is an aggregate check — it does not verify individual ticket payouts. If the ZK circuit assigns incorrect payouts to individual tickets (e.g., one ticket gets more and another less), the aggregate check would still pass. Individual payout correctness relies entirely on the ZK circuit and Merkle tree structure. The on-chain contract only enforces the aggregate invariant.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market has 2 winning yes tickets. Correct payouts: ticket0 = 5 ETH, ticket1 = 5 ETH. totalLiability = 10 ETH.
Step 2: ZK circuit assigns: ticket0 = 8 ETH, ticket1 = 2 ETH. poolYes = 10 ETH, poolNo = 0. totalLiability = 10 ETH.
Step 3: Aggregate check passes: poolYes + poolNo = 10 = totalLiability.
Step 4: Ticket0 holder claims 8 ETH (3 ETH more than deserved). Ticket1 holder claims 2 ETH (3 ETH less).
Step 5: Total is still 10 ETH, but distribution is unfair.
preconditions: ZK circuit has a bug in individual payout calculation.
Aggregate totals still satisfy the invariant.

title: MarketFactory.createMarket: No maxCommitments validation at factory level allows 0 which defaults to MAX_COMMITMENTS_LIMIT -> unfair_treatment
root_cause: createMarket passes params.maxCommitments directly to initialize without validation. RevealMarket.initialize (line 260-261) converts 0 to MAX_COMMITMENTS_LIMIT (16384). This is by design but means the factory owner can silently create markets with very large commitment limits (up to 16384 tickets) without any explicit cap at the factory level. While this is documented behavior, it could lead to markets with unexpectedly large escrow requirements relative to the protocol pool's capacity.
trigger_scenario: Factory owner creates a market with maxCommitments=0
initialize sets maxCommitments to MAX_COMMITMENTS_LIMIT (64*256 = 16384)
If ticketSize is large, total potential escrow could exceed protocol pool capacity
protocolLiabilityCap would need to be set appropriately, but there's no enforcement that cap <= pool balance
preconditions: Factory owner creates market with maxCommitments=0 or very large value

title: RevealMarket._onlyRelayerOrFactoryOwner: Relayer owner change after market creation allows unexpected access -> fund_loss
root_cause: _onlyRelayerOrFactoryOwner (line 223-229) dynamically reads RelayerEscrow(relayerEscrow).owner() and IOwnable(factory).owner() on each call. If the relayer escrow's ownership is transferred (via Ownable2Step.transferOwnership + acceptOwnership), the new relayer owner gains the onlyRelayerOrFactoryOwner privilege for all markets using that relayer. This includes the ability to call refund() to refund tickets in cancelled markets. While this is by design (the relayer owner should have this privilege), an unintended ownership transfer could give a malicious actor the ability to front-run legitimate refunds or grief users.
trigger_scenario: RelayerEscrow ownership is transferred to a new address (legitimate rotation or compromise)
New relayer owner gains onlyRelayerOrFactoryOwner privilege on all associated markets
In cancelled markets, new owner can call refund() to trigger refunds to ticket owners
Since refund always sends to the ticket owner (not the caller), this is not directly exploitable for theft
However, the new owner could selectively refuse to process refunds (griefing), though users can use refundSelf or refundTicket
preconditions: RelayerEscrow ownership is transferred
Markets exist that use this relayer

title: MarketFactory.setRelayerCommitsPaused: Large activeRelayers array could exceed block gas limit -> dos
root_cause: setRelayerCommitsPaused (line 405-422) iterates through ALL activeRelayers in batches of MAX_RELAYER_PAUSE_BATCH (64). Each batch makes up to 64 external calls (setCommitsPaused + commitsPaused verification). The function processes ALL batches in a single transaction using a while loop. If activeRelayers is very large (e.g., 1000 relayers), the function would make ~2000 external calls in one transaction, potentially exceeding the block gas limit. However, the manual batch function setRelayerCommitsPausedBatch exists as a fallback. Also, each _activateRelayer is ref-counted, and in practice the number of unique active relayers would be small (likely 1-3).
trigger_scenario: Over time, many unique relayers are activated (e.g., one per market with different relayers)
activeRelayers grows to hundreds of entries
Factory owner calls setRelayerCommitsPaused(true) in an emergency
The while loop iterates all relayers in batches of 64, making 2 external calls per relayer
Transaction exceeds block gas limit and reverts
Owner must fall back to setRelayerCommitsPausedBatch to pause relayers in smaller chunks
Emergency response is delayed
preconditions: Large number of unique active relayers (unlikely in practice, typically 1-3)
Block gas limit constrains total calls

title: RevealMarket: totalEscrow tracks net (post-rake) amounts but refund returns full ticketSize -> refund over-pays from market balance
root_cause: When a commit is made, totalEscrow increases by net = ticketSize - rake, and rakeCollected increases by rake. The market's token balance equals totalEscrow + rakeCollected = N * ticketSize. When the market enters Cancelled phase and refunds are enabled, refundTicket/refund/refundSelf each refund the full ticketSize (not net). This means each refund returns ticketSize tokens, which is correct because the user paid ticketSize. The market holds exactly N * ticketSize tokens (assuming no external transfers), so refunding all N tickets at ticketSize each exactly depletes the balance. The rake is effectively returned to users on cancellation, which is the intended behavior -- users should get full refunds on market cancellation. This is not a vulnerability but a deliberate design decision.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: 10 users commit with ticketSize=100, rakeBps=500 (5%). Market holds 1000 tokens.
Step 2: totalEscrow = 10 * 95 = 950, rakeCollected = 10 * 5 = 50.
Step 3: Market is cancelled. refundTicket refunds ticketSize=100 per ticket.
Step 4: 10 refunds * 100 = 1000 tokens needed. Market has 1000 tokens. Exact match.
Step 5: Protocol loses the 50 tokens of rake it would have collected, but users are made whole.
preconditions: Market enters Cancelled phase

title: RevealMarket: Settlement surplus forwarding sends totalEscrow + rakeCollected - totalLiability to protocolPool -> rake is captured correctly only if totalLiability < totalEscrow + rakeCollected
root_cause: In _finalizeSettlement, after settlement: (1) rakeAmount is set to rakeCollected. (2) If totalLiability > balance, protocolPool.draw() is called. (3) The surplus (balance - totalLiability) is transferred to protocolPool. The market balance before settlement = totalEscrow + rakeCollected (net tickets + accumulated rake). If totalLiability <= totalEscrow, the surplus = totalEscrow + rakeCollected - totalLiability >= rakeCollected. The full rake is forwarded to protocolPool as part of the surplus, plus any excess from totalEscrow - totalLiability. If totalLiability > totalEscrow (possible when the protocol pool tops up), the surplus could be less than rakeCollected or even zero. In the extreme case where totalLiability > totalEscrow + rakeCollected, the protocolPool must cover the entire deficit including absorbing the rake. The rake is always forwarded to the pool regardless.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: 10 tickets at 100, rakeBps=500. totalEscrow=950, rakeCollected=50. Market balance=1000.
Step 2: Settlement determines totalLiability=900. surplus = 1000 - 900 = 100 (includes 50 rake + 50 unused escrow). 100 sent to pool.
Step 3: Alternative: totalLiability=1200 > totalEscrow(950). deficit = 1200 - 1000 = 200. protocolPool.draw(200). balance = 1200. surplus = 1200 - 1200 = 0.
Step 4: In case 3, the rake (50 tokens already in the balance) was effectively consumed to partially cover the liability, reducing the protocol pool draw from 250 to 200.
preconditions: Settlement phase reached

title: RelayerEscrow.deposit: Fee-on-transfer check uses balance difference but does not guard against rebase tokens -> balance desync over time
root_cause: The deposit functions check received == amount (balance after - balance before == amount), which correctly catches fee-on-transfer tokens. However, rebase tokens (like stETH) can change balances outside of transfers. If the collateral token is a rebase token, the escrow's balance could increase or decrease between transactions, causing accountedCollateral to become permanently desynced from the actual balance. For positive rebases, excess collateral would appear. For negative rebases, accountedCollateral > balanceOf, meaning some users cannot withdraw (first-come-first-serve drain). The contract uses a single immutable COLLATERAL_TOKEN, so the risk depends on which token is chosen at deployment. USDC and standard ERC20s are not rebase tokens.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Escrow is deployed with a rebase token (e.g., stETH).
Step 2: User deposits 100. balances[user]=100, accountedCollateral=100, actual balance=100.
Step 3: Negative rebase: actual balance drops to 99. accountedCollateral=100 > balance=99.
Step 4: User tries to withdraw 100. Transfer would fail because escrow only has 99.
Step 5: If multiple users, last withdrawer is shortchanged.
preconditions: COLLATERAL_TOKEN is a rebase token

title: RevealMarket._verifyBatchProof: Accumulated settledEscrowSum across batches can be manipulated via per-batch signal values -> TotalsMismatch bypass if circuit allows flexibility
root_cause: In _verifyBatchProof (lines 843-846), settledEscrowSum, settledLiabilitySum, settledPoolYesSum, and settledPoolNoSum accumulate signals[3], signals[4], signals[6], and signals[7] from each batch proof. The per-batch values are proven by the ZK circuit, so they cannot be arbitrarily chosen. However, the on-chain code does NOT validate that signals[3] (batch escrow) equals the expected escrow for that specific batch (batchCounts[i] * netTicketSize). The only aggregate check is `settledEscrowSum != totalEscrow` at line 439. If the ZK circuit does not independently constrain per-batch escrow to match the exact ticket count * net value for that batch, an attacker who can generate valid proofs with incorrect per-batch distributions could shift liability between batches. The circuit integrity is the defense here -- if the circuit properly constrains these values, this is not exploitable.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market has 2 batches: batch 0 with 256 tickets, batch 1 with 1 ticket.
Step 2: Attacker generates a valid proof for batch 0 claiming totalEscrow = (256 + 1) * netTicket (all escrow in batch 0).
Step 3: Attacker generates a valid proof for batch 1 claiming totalEscrow = 0.
Step 4: settledEscrowSum = (257 * netTicket) + 0 = totalEscrow, passes TotalsMismatch check.
Step 5: However, the per-batch liability could be skewed, affecting settlement surplus/deficit calculations.
preconditions: ZK circuit must allow per-batch totalEscrow to differ from the actual batch ticket sum
Attacker must be able to generate valid Groth16 proofs with manipulated signals

title: RevealMarket.verifyAndSettleBatched: Multi-tx batch accumulation allows oracle to settle batches in separate transactions, each verified independently -> Accumulated sums bypass per-batch economic checks
root_cause: verifyAndSettleBatched can be called multiple times before all batches are settled. Each call accumulates settledEscrowSum, settledLiabilitySum, etc. The final check `settledEscrowSum != totalEscrow` only happens when `settledBatchCount == batchCount` (lines 438-440). Between calls, the accumulated sums are in intermediate states. There is no per-batch escrow validation -- the contract doesn't know how much escrow each batch should contribute. The only constraint is that the ZK proof is valid for each batch's Merkle root. If the ZK circuit allows a batch to claim more escrow than it actually has (e.g., by manipulating the totalEscrow signal for a batch), intermediate accumulation could allow one batch to subsidize another. The aggregate check catches any discrepancy, but per-batch sums are not individually validated.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market has 2 batches. Batch 0 has 256 tickets with 1 ETH net each (256 ETH escrow). Batch 1 has 1 ticket with 1 ETH net (1 ETH escrow). Total escrow = 257 ETH.
Step 2: Oracle submits proof for batch 0 with signals[3] = 257 ETH (claiming all escrow for batch 0).
Step 3: Oracle submits proof for batch 1 with signals[3] = 0 ETH.
Step 4: settledEscrowSum = 257 + 0 = 257 = totalEscrow. Check passes.
Step 5: The liability and pool distributions could be skewed between batches.
Step 6: If circuit properly constrains per-batch values, this attack is impossible.
preconditions: ZK circuit must not properly constrain per-batch escrow to match the batch's actual ticket count * net ticket value

title: RevealMarket.verifyAndSettle: Single-batch path checks signals[3] != totalEscrow directly but does NOT check signals[4] (totalLiability) against any on-chain value -> Circuit is sole enforcer of liability correctness
root_cause: In verifyAndSettle (lines 403-409), the code checks: signals[0] == batchRoots[0], signals[1] == marketId, signals[2] == winningOutcomeId, signals[3] == totalEscrow, signals[5] == rakeBps, signals[8] == circuitHash, signals[9] == 0. Notably, signals[4] (totalLiability), signals[6] (poolYes), and signals[7] (poolNo) are NOT checked against any on-chain values. They are passed directly to _finalizeSettlement which only checks poolYes + poolNo == totalLiability (line 716) and totalLiability <= totalEscrow + protocolLiabilityCap (line 723). The correctness of these values relies entirely on the ZK circuit. If the circuit is sound, these values are proven correct. If the circuit has a bug allowing arbitrary liability, the market could settle with inflated totalLiability, drawing from the protocol pool unnecessarily. This is a fundamental trust assumption of ZK-verified settlement.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market has totalEscrow = 100 ETH, protocolLiabilityCap = 500 ETH.
Step 2: Honest circuit would compute totalLiability = 80 ETH.
Step 3: Buggy circuit allows oracle to prove totalLiability = 500 ETH.
Step 4: signals[3] = 100 (matches totalEscrow, passes check). signals[4] = 500. signals[6] = 500, signals[7] = 0.
Step 5: poolYes + poolNo = 500 == totalLiability. Passes invariant.
Step 6: 500 <= 100 + 500. Passes coverage check.
Step 7: deficit = 500 - 100 = 400. Drawn from pool. Market now has 500 ETH for claims.
Step 8: Attacker claims 500 ETH worth of fake winning tickets. Protocol pool loses 400 ETH.
preconditions: ZK circuit must have a soundness bug allowing arbitrary totalLiability values to pass proof verification

title: ProtocolPool.maxRedeemable: Rounding in mulDiv for underwater inverse share calculation -> fund_loss
root_cause: In `maxRedeemable` (line 324), when the pool is underwater, the inverse calculation `Math.mulDiv(idle, totalShares, balance)` converts idle liquidity to equivalent shares. `Math.mulDiv` rounds down by default. This could cause `maxRedeemable` to return a share count whose `convertToAssets` value exceeds available idle liquidity, causing `lpWithdraw` to revert with `InsufficientIdleLiquidity`. This is a view-function inconsistency, not a fund loss, but could cause UX issues where maxRedeemable claims a value is withdrawable but the actual withdrawal fails.
trigger_scenario: Pool: 10 assets, 30 shares (underwater). idle = 10, reservedTotal = 0.
maxRedeemable: balance(10) < totalShares(30), so returns mulDiv(10, 30, 10) = 30 shares.
LP calls lpWithdraw(30): convertToAssets(30) = mulDiv(30, 10, 30) = 10 assets. idle = 10. 10 <= 10. OK.
Actually consistent here. But with non-round numbers:
Pool: 7 assets, 20 shares. maxRedeemable: mulDiv(7, 20, 7) = 20. convertToAssets(20) = mulDiv(20, 7, 20) = 7. OK.
Pool: 7 assets, 13 shares. maxRedeemable: mulDiv(7, 13, 7) = 13. convertToAssets(13) = mulDiv(13, 7, 13) = 7. OK.
Rounding seems consistent when totalShares cancels. Low risk.
preconditions: Pool is underwater
Non-trivial rounding exists in the division

title: ProtocolPool.draw: Balance invariant check after transfer is incomplete for re-entrant tokens -> fund_loss
root_cause: The `draw()` function (lines 172-182) performs multiple balance checks after `safeTransfer`: it verifies the pool was debited exactly `amount` and the market received at least `amount`. However, it also checks `balanceAfter > balance` (line 176) which would revert if the balance somehow increased. This is to guard against weird token behavior. The `nonReentrant` modifier protects against reentrancy within ProtocolPool, but `_safeTransferExactOut` in `lpWithdraw` also has robust checks. The draw function's check is thorough. However, if the collateral token has callbacks (ERC777-style), the market receiving tokens could call back into ProtocolPool. The `nonReentrant` guard prevents this.
trigger_scenario: Market calls draw(market, 100).
safeTransfer sends 100 tokens to market.
If token has transfer hooks (ERC777), the market's tokensReceived callback fires.
Market tries to re-enter ProtocolPool (e.g., call draw again).
nonReentrant prevents re-entry. No issue.
But market could call a non-reentrant-guarded function like reserveLiability.
reserveLiability reads COLLATERAL_TOKEN.balanceOf(address(this)) which now reflects the transfer.
The balance check in draw hasn't completed yet, but reserveLiability sees the reduced balance.
reserveLiability would likely revert with InsufficientPool (lower balance). Safe.
preconditions: Collateral token has transfer callbacks (not standard ERC20)
Market contract exploits callback to interact with pool

title: MarketFactory.updateMarketRelayer: Relayer rotation guard checks phase+tickets but does not prevent rotation after commitDeadline -> griefing
root_cause: updateMarketRelayer (line 272) checks rm.phase() != Phase.Commit || rm.nextTicketId() != 0. This allows rotation only when phase is Commit AND no tickets have been committed. But it does NOT check whether block.timestamp < commitDeadline. If the commit deadline has passed but lockBatches hasn't been called yet (market is still in Commit phase with 0 tickets), the relayer can be rotated. This is safe since there are no user funds at risk (no commits exist). However, after rotation, the market is registered on a new relayer that has no user context for this empty market.
trigger_scenario: Market is created with commit deadline T
No users commit before T
After T, market is still in Commit phase with 0 tickets (no one called lockBatches or enableRefunds)
Factory owner calls updateMarketRelayer — guard passes (phase is Commit, nextTicketId is 0)
Relayer is rotated — no harm since no user funds exist
Eventually enableRefunds is called (or market is abandoned)
preconditions: Market has no commitments
Commit deadline has passed
lockBatches or enableRefunds has not yet been called

title: MarketFactory.updateMarketVerifier: Verifier rotation allowed during Commit phase after commitments exist if circuitHash unchanged -> unfair_treatment
root_cause: RevealMarket.setVerifier (line 666-675) allows verifier rotation during Commit phase. If commitments.length != 0, it only requires newCircuitHash == circuitHash (line 671). This means the verifier contract itself can be swapped to a different implementation (with a different verifying key) as long as the circuitHash remains the same. Users who committed under the old verifier may find their proofs no longer valid under the new verifier if the verifying key changed (different VK means different valid proofs for the same circuit). However, the prover (off-chain) generates proofs using the current VK at settlement time, not at commit time, so this only affects the verifier's ability to verify — not the committed data itself.
trigger_scenario: Users commit tickets to market M with verifier V1 (VK1, circuitHash C)
Factory owner calls updateMarketVerifier(M, V2, C) where V2 has VK2 but same circuitHash C
setVerifier passes: commitments.length > 0 but newCircuitHash == circuitHash
Market is locked, oracle locks batches referencing V2's verifyingKeyHash
Proofs must be generated against V2's VK2, not V1's VK1
If prover uses the correct (new) VK, settlement succeeds — this is the intended flow
No user funds are at risk since the circuit logic (circuitHash) didn't change
preconditions: Market has commitments
New verifier has same circuitHash but different verifyingKey
Factory owner rotates verifier during commit phase

title: RevealMarket.setCommitsPaused: No phase check allows pausing commits during Settled/Cancelled phases -> griefing
root_cause: RevealMarket.setCommitsPaused (line 694-697) has no phase check — it can be called in any phase. During Settled or Cancelled phases, commits are already impossible (commitWithAuthorization checks phase == Commit), so setting commitsPaused is a no-op functionally. However, enableRefunds already sets commitsPaused = true (line 484). If the factory owner calls setCommitsPaused(false) on a Cancelled market, it would clear the commitsPaused flag, but commits would still fail due to the phase check. This is harmless but could confuse off-chain monitoring that checks commitsPaused as a signal.
trigger_scenario: Market is settled or cancelled
Factory owner calls setMarketCommitsPaused(market, true) — commitsPaused is set to true
No functional impact since commitWithAuthorization already checks phase == Commit
Factory owner calls setMarketCommitsPaused(market, false) on a cancelled market
commitsPaused is cleared, but refunds still work and commits still fail due to phase check
preconditions: Market is in Settled or Cancelled phase

title: RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization: abi.encodePacked with adjacent address fields creates collision risk -> signature forgery
root_cause: The commit digest in commitWithAuthorization uses abi.encodePacked with the field sequence: address(this) (20 bytes) | marketId (uint256, 32 bytes) | ticketId (uint256, 32 bytes) | commitment (bytes32, 32 bytes) | auth.user (address, 20 bytes) | nonce (uint256, 32 bytes) | .... Because both address fields are 20 bytes and sit adjacent to fixed-size 32-byte fields, there is no packing ambiguity between these specific types -- addresses are always 20 bytes and uint256/bytes32 are always 32 bytes. However, the first field (address, 20 bytes) followed by marketId (uint256, 32 bytes) means that the leading 12 zero bytes of marketId could be confused with the trailing 12 bytes of a padded address if abi.encode were used instead. In practice, since all types here are fixed-width, abi.encodePacked produces a deterministic concatenation with no collision. Nevertheless, the use of abi.encodePacked when abi.encode could be used introduces unnecessary fragility -- a future refactor adding a variable-length field would silently create collision risk.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Observe that address(this) is 20 bytes, followed by uint256 marketId (32 bytes).
Step 2: Attempt to construct a second set of inputs that produces the same packed bytes.
Step 3: Because all types are fixed-width (address=20B, uint256=32B, bytes32=32B), no two distinct input tuples can produce the same packed output.
Step 4: Collision is not achievable with current types, but the pattern is fragile.
preconditions: All CommitAuth fields must remain fixed-width types

title: RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization: rakeBps=0 is valid at initialization -> all tickets have zero rake by design
root_cause: The initialize function checks params.rakeBps > 10_000 (revert if over 100%), but allows rakeBps = 0. With rakeBps = 0, every commit has rake = 0 and net = ticketSize. This is a valid configuration (no-fee market), but it means rakeCollected will always be 0 and the settlement surplus forwarding at line 736 (tokenBalance - totalLiability) may include no rake. This is a design choice, not a bug, but should be explicitly documented as intentional.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Initialize market with rakeBps = 0.
Step 2: All commits have rake = 0, net = ticketSize.
Step 3: totalEscrow = N * ticketSize, rakeCollected = 0.
Step 4: No protocol revenue from this market.
preconditions: rakeBps == 0 at initialization

title: RelayerEscrow.commitOnBehalf: Transfer then commitWithAuthorization ordering means escrow cannot verify market actually stored the commitment -> silent commit failure
root_cause: In commitOnBehalf, the escrow transfers tokens to the market, then calls commitWithAuthorization. If commitWithAuthorization reverts (e.g., due to expired commitment, invalid signature, or paused state), the entire transaction reverts, and the token transfer is also rolled back. This is correct -- Solidity's atomic transaction model ensures all-or-nothing behavior. The escrow does not need to separately verify the commitment was stored because a revert undoes everything. However, if the market's commitWithAuthorization were to silently succeed without actually storing the commitment (e.g., a malicious market that accepts tokens but does nothing), the user's balance would be debited but no ticket would exist. The allowedMarket + _isValidMarket check mitigates this, but a compromised factory could register such a market.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Factory is compromised and registers a malicious market that passes _isValidMarket checks.
Step 2: Malicious market's commitWithAuthorization accepts the token transfer but does not store the commitment.
Step 3: User's escrow balance is debited, tokens are in the malicious market, but no ticket exists.
Step 4: User has no way to claim or get refunded.
preconditions: Factory must be compromised to register a malicious market

title: RevealMarket.commitWithAuthorization: EIP-191 prefix + abi.encodePacked creates ambiguous hash if backend signs using EIP-712 -> signature scheme mismatch
root_cause: The contract uses toEthSignedMessageHash (EIP-191 personal_sign: '\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n32' prefix) applied to the keccak256 of the encodePacked data. If the backend were to sign using EIP-712 (\x19\x01 prefix + domain separator + struct hash), the signatures would be incompatible. This is a backend implementation concern, not a smart contract vulnerability. The contract is consistent: it always expects EIP-191 signatures. The backend must match this expectation. If the backend signs with a different scheme, all commits would fail (fail-safe behavior).
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Contract expects EIP-191 signature of the commit digest.
Step 2: Backend signs using EIP-712 with a domain separator.
Step 3: Signature recovery in the contract produces a different address.
Step 4: All commits revert with InvalidSignature.
Step 5: This is a configuration error, not an attack vector.
preconditions: Backend misconfigured to use wrong signing scheme

title: RelayerEscrow.approveCommitAuthorization: User approval not time-bounded -> stale approvals can be consumed indefinitely
root_cause: When a user calls approveCommitAuthorization, the approval is stored as a boolean in approvedCommitAuthorizations[user][authHash] = true. This approval has no expiry. The authHash includes auth.expiry, so different expiry values produce different hashes. However, the user's approval persists forever until consumed by commitOnBehalf. If the user approves a commit authorization but the relayer never executes it, the approval remains in storage indefinitely. A future relayer (after ownership transfer via Ownable2Step) could consume this stale approval. However, the commitment parameters (including expiry) are baked into the hash, and commitWithAuthorization checks auth.expiry < block.timestamp. So a stale approval for an expired authorization would cause commitWithAuthorization to revert. The auth.expiry provides an effective time bound at the market level, even though the escrow approval has no explicit expiry.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: User approves commit authorization with auth.expiry = T + 3600 (1 hour).
Step 2: Relayer does not execute the commit within 1 hour.
Step 3: At T + 7200, a new relayer becomes owner and tries to execute the stale approval.
Step 4: commitOnBehalf succeeds (approval exists), but commitWithAuthorization checks auth.expiry (T+3600) < block.timestamp (T+7200) and reverts with CommitExpired.
Step 5: The stale approval is NOT consumed (the revert rolls back everything). It remains in storage but cannot be used for the expired authorization.
Step 6: However, if the same authorization parameters (with a different, future expiry) were used, a different authHash would be computed, so the stale approval for the old expiry would not apply.
preconditions: Relayer ownership changes after user approves commit authorization

title: RevealMarket._finalizeSettlement: Surplus forwarding to protocolPool includes rakeCollected -> Protocol receives rake + surplus together
root_cause: In _finalizeSettlement (lines 713-752), the contract computes `required = totalLiability_` (line 722), draws deficit from pool if needed (lines 726-729), then computes surplus as `tokenBalance - totalLiability_` (line 736). The market's token balance includes the rake amount (rakeCollected, stored at line 315). Since `totalEscrow = sum(ticketSize - rake)` and the market holds `sum(ticketSize)`, the actual balance is `totalEscrow + rakeCollected`. The surplus calculation at line 736 will include the rakeCollected in the surplus: `surplus = (totalEscrow + rakeCollected) - totalLiability_`. This means the rake is forwarded to protocolPool as part of the surplus transfer. The `rakeAmount` storage variable is set to `rakeCollected` (line 721) for accounting but the tokens are sent to protocolPool. This appears intentional -- rake goes to the protocol pool. However, if `totalLiability_ > totalEscrow`, the deficit draw covers the difference, and then surplus = (totalEscrow + deficit + rakeCollected) - totalLiability_ = rakeCollected. So rake always flows to protocolPool. This is by design.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market collects 100 tickets at 1 ETH each with 2% rake. totalEscrow = 98 ETH, rakeCollected = 2 ETH, balance = 100 ETH.
Step 2: Settlement determines totalLiability = 95 ETH (all bettors on winning side).
Step 3: required = 95 ETH. Balance = 100 ETH. No deficit draw needed.
Step 4: surplus = 100 - 95 = 5 ETH (includes 2 ETH rake + 3 ETH actual surplus).
Step 5: 5 ETH sent to protocolPool. Market retains 95 ETH for claims.
preconditions: Normal market operation

title: RevealMarket._finalizeSettlement: Settlement invariant poolYes + poolNo == totalLiability does not enforce poolYes/poolNo correspondence to actual winning/losing bets -> Incorrect payout distribution
root_cause: The settlement invariant check at line 716 (`poolYes_ + poolNo_ != totalLiability_`) ensures the sum is correct but does not verify that poolYes corresponds to bets on outcome 0 and poolNo to outcome 1 (or vice versa). The public signals include winningOutcomeId (signals[2]) which is checked against the on-chain `winningOutcomeId` (lines 404, 831), so the circuit should be computing payouts for the correct outcome. The circuit is the sole enforcer of correctness in the poolYes/poolNo split. If the circuit has a bug where poolYes and poolNo are swapped, settlement would finalize with incorrect distribution, but `totalLiability` would still be correct, meaning the market holds enough funds. Claims would fail or succeed incorrectly depending on individual ticket matching.
trigger_scenario: Step 1: Market has bets: 60% on outcome 0, 40% on outcome 1. Outcome 0 wins.
Step 2: Circuit correctly calculates poolYes (total payouts to outcome 0 bettors). Oracle proves this.
Step 3: If circuit has a bug and swaps poolYes/poolNo, totalLiability is still correct (same sum).
Step 4: _finalizeSettlement passes. Phase becomes Settled.
Step 5: Individual claims still verify against Merkle leaves which encode per-ticket payout, so the swap in pool totals doesn't directly affect individual claims.
Step 6: However, if a future version uses poolYes/poolNo for payout calculations, this could be exploited.
preconditions: Circuit must have a bug swapping poolYes and poolNo

title: RevealMarket._finalizeSettlement: LiabilityExceedsCoverage check uses protocolLiabilityCap from storage which can differ from ProtocolPool's liabilityCap -> Coverage gap
root_cause: In _finalizeSettlement, line 723 checks `required > totalEscrow_ + protocolLiabilityCap`. The `protocolLiabilityCap` is the market's own stored value. When `draw()` is called on the ProtocolPool (line 729), the pool checks `newConsumed > liabilityCap[market]` (ProtocolPool line 158).
